claim.title: execute_graph's preview-cache try_get -> _eager_execute -> store/pin is a non-atomic RMW on the process-global cache; a concurrent extend can overwrite a sibling request's freshly-stored node frames (last-writer-wins on the whole entry)
claim.location: src/haute/executor.py:918-919 (try_get under lock then released), 966-1029 (extend: execute then merge {**prev_outputs, **eager_outputs} then store+pin), 1061-1077 (miss path store+pin)
claim.failure_scenario: Two concurrent requests A and B share the same fingerprint fp (same graph/source/row_limit/contracts) but different target nodes (different ancestor coverage). Both call _preview_cache.try_get(fp) and both observe the same prev_outputs snapshot (or both miss). Each runs _eager_execute for its own target, then computes merged = {**prev_outputs, **own_fresh_outputs} from the SNAPSHOT it read, and calls _preview_cache.store(fp, eager_outputs=merged, ...). The second store to land overwrites the first: A's freshly-materialised nodes that B did not recompute are dropped from the cache entry because B's merged was built from the pre-A snapshot. Result: a subsequent request that needs A's nodes sees a partial-hit miss and re-executes (a correctness-neutral but silent perf regression and a heavy-DataFrame re-materialisation), and during the window the cache entry's node set is non-deterministic. The merge logic is correct per-call (fresh wins on overlap), so no STALE frame is served; the defect is lost work + non-deterministic entry contents under interleave, plus the pin/unpin pair is balanced only because each request pins and unpins its own fp in try/finally (no leak).
claim.repro_strategy: Drive two threads through execute_graph on the same graph/source/row_limit with distinct target_node_ids that have disjoint extra ancestors, after seeding a small shared cache entry. Use a barrier so both observe the same try_get snapshot before either stores (monkeypatch _eager_execute to block on an Event between read and store). Assert the final cached entry is missing one thread's recomputed node (i.e. set(cache.try_get(fp)['eager_outputs']) does not contain both targets' exclusive ancestors), demonstrating the lost-write.

verdict.evidence: The claim's load-bearing precondition -- "two concurrent requests A and B share the same fingerprint fp ... but different target nodes" -- does not hold for any concurrent driver. The full census of execute_graph call sites is exactly three (src/haute/executor.py): cli/_run.py:55 (CLI, single-threaded, no target), routes/pipeline.py:530 (the ONLY concurrent HTTP driver), and _scaffold.py:1210 (generated deploy validation, single-threaded, no target). The preview route ALWAYS calls execute_graph(..., target_preview_only=True). _preview_projection_cache_suffix (executor.py:654-655) appends f":preview_target_only={target_node_id!r}" to the cache-key suffix whenever target_preview_only is True; that suffix is extra_keys[0] (executor.py:901-904) which graph_fingerprint mixes into the digest (_cache.py:429-432). So distinct targets => distinct fp => distinct cache entries. The non-atomic try_get->_eager_execute->store RMW (correctly identified as lock-free across the sequence) therefore writes to SEPARATE entries and cannot last-writer-wins-drop a sibling frame. Additionally, same-target concurrent previews share the _preview_supersession_key (pipeline.py:202-218, which includes node_id) so SupersessionCoordinator serialises them (one running per key) -- they do not race either. Repro output (exit 0): suffix(node_a)=":preview_target_only='node_a':initial_col_limit=200" vs suffix(node_b)=":preview_target_only='node_b':initial_col_limit=200"; fp(node_a)=v5:0666d... vs fp(node_b)=v5:55897... (DISTINCT). Both threads were forced (via a 2-party Barrier injected into _eager_execute) to complete their try_get read before either stored -- log shows "both threads entered _eager_execute (post-try_get): calls=['node_a','node_b']" with two separate preview_cache_miss lines (fingerprint=v5:0666d target=node_a; fingerprint=v5:55897 target=node_b) -- yet entry[fp_a] nodes stayed ['node_a'] before AND after B's store: "OK: distinct entries; target_a's frames survive target_b's store (no drop)." No path calls execute_graph with target_preview_only=False and a varying target concurrently, so the empty-suffix collision case the claim would need is unreachable.
verdict.repro_outcome: Exit 0 (refutation repro). PART 1: reconstructing fp exactly as execute_graph does for two distinct targets under target_preview_only=True yields DISTINCT fingerprints (v5:0666d... vs v5:55897...), because the suffix embeds the target id. PART 2: drove two real threads through execute_graph(..., target_preview_only=True) for siblings node_a/node_b with a Barrier inside _eager_execute forcing both to pass try_get before either stores; both wrote to SEPARATE cache entries (two preview_cache_miss lines) and target_a's entry remained {'node_a'} after target_b stored -- no sibling frame dropped. Assertions that would have SUPPORTED the claim (same fp for distinct targets; entry[fp_a] changing after B's store; target_a missing from its own entry) all held the refuting direction.

claim.title: _compile_preamble_cached holds _preamble_lock only on lru_cache MISS while it mutates process-global sys.path and evicts sys.modules['utility']; concurrent lru_cache HITS (or any other importer) run unsynchronised against that window
claim.location: src/haute/executor.py:343-377 (_compile_preamble_cached; lock window 369-377), 249-281 (_evict_utility_import_state + _prioritise_preamble_import_paths)
claim.failure_scenario: On an lru_cache miss for a utility-importing preamble, the worker takes _preamble_lock, calls _prioritise_preamble_import_paths (rewrites sys.path[:] in place), then _evict_utility_import_state (deletes sys.modules['utility*'] and unlinks pyc), then exec()s the preamble which (re)imports utility. A SECOND thread whose preamble text is identical and already cached returns via the lru_cache HIT fast-path WITHOUT taking _preamble_lock (the lock is only inside _compile_preamble_cached's body, reached on miss); but more dangerously, a different code path importing 'utility' (e.g. a node builder, or a second DISTINCT preamble whose miss also runs) can be mid-`import utility` exactly while thread 1 has deleted utility from sys.modules. This is the documented KeyError-in-importlib._bootstrap window. Because two DIFFERENT preamble keys both go through the miss path they DO serialise on _preamble_lock, but sys.path reprioritisation by a non-utility preamble (which also takes the lock for its short window per the module comment) versus a concurrent utility import that does NOT take the lock can still bind a 'utility' module resolved against a transiently different sys.path ordering — silently importing the wrong utility.py (e.g. cwd/utility.py vs pipeline_dir/utility.py) into the namespace.
claim.repro_strategy: Code-trace: show (a) the lru_cache HIT path in _compile_preamble -> _compile_preamble_cached returns before entering the `with _preamble_lock` body, and (b) sys.path[:] / del sys.modules['utility'] inside the locked block are process-global mutations observable by any thread not holding the lock. A timing repro would monkeypatch _exec_preamble_namespace to sleep mid-exec while a second thread does `import utility` against two utility.py files at different sys.path priorities and assert the bound module differs from the single-threaded result; inherently flaky, hence testable=false.

verdict.evidence: The claim's escalation requires an "unlocked code path importing utility" (a node builder, or a concurrent utility import that does NOT take _preamble_lock). No such path exists. (1) Whole-tree Grep of src/haute for `^\s*(import utility|from utility)` => "No matches found": there is NO production `import utility` statement; utility is imported only by user-preamble TEXT run via exec() inside _exec_preamble_namespace, which executor.py:377 calls only inside `with _preamble_lock:`. (2) src/haute/_builders.py has ZERO references to "utility" — node builders consume the already-resolved preamble_ns dict, never re-import. (3) The ONLY mutators of utility import state in the whole tree are executor.py:254 `del sys.modules[mod_name]`, :279 `sys.path[:] = ...`, :280 `sys.path.insert(0, path)`; Grep confirms `del sys.modules[` and `sys.path[:]` each appear exactly once, both inside _evict_utility_import_state / _prioritise_preamble_import_paths, both reached only from inside the locked block (executor.py:369-377). (4) Line 369 wraps line 370 (_prioritise_preamble_import_paths) UNCONDITIONALLY — non-utility preambles also hold the lock for their path-rewrite window, so the claimed "non-utility rewrite vs concurrent unlocked utility import" race has no second actor. (5) _cache.py fingerprint helpers called OUTSIDE the lock (preamble_imports_utility, preamble_execution_fingerprint) only AST-parse and hash files — they never import or touch sys.path/sys.modules. The lru_cache HIT-skips-lock fact is true but harmless: a HIT returns a pre-built materialized dict via functools.lru_cache without entering the body, performing zero import-state ops, so it neither mutates nor observes transient state. Executed repro output: "max critical-section occupancy: 1 (expected 1)"; "per-thread utility origin: {'D':'pipeline_dir','A':'pipeline_dir','B':'pipeline_dir','C':'pipeline_dir'}"; "worker errors: none" — with 4 concurrent DISTINCT utility-importing preamble misses and two utility.py at different sys.path priorities, the critical section stayed single-occupant and every thread bound the correct pipeline_dir/utility.py.
verdict.repro_outcome: Exit 0 (claim refuted). Source-invariant checks passed (exactly one `del sys.modules[` and one `sys.path[:]` in executor.py, both inside the locked helpers; prioritise/evict/exec all ordered inside the `with _preamble_lock` block). Behavioural check: 4 concurrent threads each compiling a DISTINCT utility-importing preamble keyed to pipeline_dir, with a competing other_dir/utility.py inserted first on sys.path; instrumented lock reported max occupancy 1, and all 4 threads read UTILITY_ORIGIN=='pipeline_dir'. No interleave and no wrong-utility binding observed.

claim.title: In-flight memory admission reserves the full per-profile LIMIT (not estimated usage) and releases it only via weakref.finalize at GC, so stale contexts the route never close() can exhaust the process-wide in-flight budget and spuriously refuse legitimate jobs
claim.location: src/haute/_execution_admission.py:430-465 (reserve + weakref.finalize(context, admission_release)), 499-543 (_reserve_in_flight_budget reserves budget.memory_limit_bytes), 546-555 (_in_flight_limit_bytes); src/haute/_execution_context.py:687-700 (release_admission/close, only caller-invoked)
claim.failure_scenario: create_admitted_execution_context reserves reservation_bytes = budget.memory_limit_bytes (the configured/adaptive LIMIT, e.g. 4GiB for LAZY_SINK) in the process-wide _IN_FLIGHT_RESERVATIONS ledger, capped at _in_flight_limit_bytes (~available-RAM minus OS reserve). Release happens through (a) ExecutionContext.release_admission()/close() if a caller explicitly invokes it, or (b) weakref.finalize(context, admission_release) when the context object is garbage-collected. Routes that build a context, hand it to execution, and return without calling close() (and keep a reference alive in a JobStore / metrics payload / closure) leave the reservation standing until GC actually collects the context. Under concurrent heavy operations (sink + training + optimiser + deploy_batch), 2-3 lingering LIMIT-sized reservations sum past _in_flight_limit_bytes, so the next admit raises ExecutionAdmissionError('in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded') even though real RSS is low (the reservations are coarse LIMITs, not usage). Conversely, because reservations are LIMIT-sized rather than usage-tracked, the ledger over-counts and refuses work that would actually fit — an availability defect, not a safety one.
claim.repro_strategy: Set HAUTE_EXECUTION_MEMORY_POLICY=fixed so LAZY_SINK limit=4GiB; patch _ram_estimate.available_ram_bytes to ~9GiB (in_flight_limit ~7GiB after default 2GiB reserve). Call create_admitted_execution_context(profile=LAZY_SINK) twice WITHOUT close() and hold both contexts in a list (defeating GC). A third call raises ExecutionAdmissionError reason='in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded' despite no real memory use. Then call ctx.close() on one and show the third now admits — proving release is gated on explicit close()/GC, not on actual completion.

verdict.evidence: Repro output: "[A] reservation size == LIMIT: 4294967296 bytes (4 GiB) -- CONFIRMED"; "[B] 3rd admit refused with 'in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded' despite ~100 B real RSS -- CONFIRMED"; "[C] reservations: before_gc=1 after_gc=1 ... weakref.finalize backstop RECLAIMS dropped-without-close() reservation". The mechanical core is TRUE: src/haute/_execution_admission.py:510 `reservation_bytes = budget.memory_limit_bytes` reserves the coarse per-profile LIMIT (not usage), and lines 511-523 refuse the next admit when the sum exceeds _in_flight_limit_bytes. BUT the claim's thesis ("released only via weakref.finalize at GC, so stale contexts the route never close() leak until GC and exhaust the budget") is FALSE on three independent grounds. (1) Every real caller of create_admitted_execution_context releases via try/finally and/or a completion/done-callback path: _explore_service.py:754-756; _optimiser_service.py:2888-2890,2953-2955,4041,4056,4983; pipeline.py:710-711,800-801 plus add_done_callback at 660-661,779-780 for the timeout-during-background case; deploy/_scorer.py:138-140; _train_service.py:588-589 (finally) and 1228,1246 (background completion/error). Holding the reservation while background work is genuinely in-flight and releasing on completion is CORRECT accounting, not a leak. (2) The specific "JobStore / metrics payload" reference the claim names is a weakref.ref (src/haute/routes/_job_lifecycle.py:64 `context_ref = weakref.ref(execution_context)`), so it cannot keep the context alive or defeat GC — the codebase is engineered against the exact scenario. (3) The weakref.finalize backstop (line 463-464) actually works: a context dropped without close() is reclaimed promptly under CPython refcounting (count was already back to 1 BEFORE gc.collect() ran), so there is no indefinite leak. The only residual true attribute — coarse LIMIT-sized reservations refusing work that would physically fit — is the deliberate, tested admission policy (see tests/test_execution_context.py:262 test_heavy_execution_admission_counts_in_flight_budget), conservative worst-case admission aligned with CLAUDE.md's "fail loudly over silent incorrectness." That is by-design availability conservatism, not the resource-leak defect asserted.
verdict.repro_outcome: Ran to completion. Sub-assertions A and B passed (reservation == 4 GiB LIMIT; third concurrent admit refused with reason 'in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded' at ~100 B real RSS). Sub-assertion C DISPROVED the leak thesis: a context built and dropped without close() had its reservation reclaimed before gc.collect() was even called (before_gc=1, after_gc=1), proving weakref.finalize is a working backstop, not a leak. Combined with code-trace of all 5 callers (all release) and the weakref.ref metrics binding, the 'stale contexts leak until GC and spuriously refuse jobs' claim is refuted.

claim.title: DataFrameExecutionCache artifact lifetime hinges on weakref.finalize of scan LazyFrames running on a GC thread; the single-unlink rule plus _release_consumed_parents keep-list can leave an artifact deleted while a derived collect still needs it, or leaked if finalize runs late (esp. Windows file-sharing)
claim.location: src/haute/_dataframe_execution_cache.py:60-69 (_release_pinned_scan), 369-391 (scan registers finalize), 527-540 (_remove_key single-unlink), 558-579 (_release_scan); src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:988-1007 (_release_consumed_parents keeps cache_backed nodes), 1419 (scan_parquet replacement after checkpoint)
claim.failure_scenario: scan(key) increments _scan_refcounts and pins the key; the returned LazyFrame gets a weakref.finalize -> _release_pinned_scan that decrements the refcount and, under the single-unlink rule, may unlink the parquet once no scan refs remain AND the entry is gone/replaced. Two coupled hazards: (1) Premature unlink — _release_consumed_parents (lazy path) deliberately keeps cache_backed nodes' LazyFrames alive, but if a cache entry is evicted/replaced (LRU max_entries=16, or store_artifact's evict_where on same-key replacement) while a DERIVED lazy plan (built from the scan but no longer holding the original scan LazyFrame after a checkpoint del) is still pending collection, _release_scan's `entry_after is None or entry_after.path != path` branch unlinks the file; a subsequent streaming_collect of the derived plan then fails with FileNotFoundError/CacheArtifactMissing. Polars Rust buffers vs Python GC timing make the 'is the original scan still referenced' question nondeterministic. (2) Leak — if finalize runs late or never (reference cycle, interpreter teardown ordering) the artifact is never unlinked, growing the temp dir unbounded; on Windows the unlink itself can raise PermissionError while the parquet is memory-mapped open, which _release_scan does not guard (path.unlink(missing_ok=True) propagates non-ENOENT OSError on win32).
claim.repro_strategy: Use a small cache (max_entries=2). Materialize node A (artifact a). scan A -> lf_a; build a derived plan d = lf_a.select(...).head(1) and DROP lf_a (del lf_a; gc.collect()) so only the derived plan references the buffers. Force eviction by materializing B and C (exceeding max_entries) so A's entry is removed. Then d.collect(). On the buggy path the artifact for A was unlinked at A's eviction (no live scan after del lf_a) and collect raises FileNotFoundError. A Windows-specific variant: hold lf_a, mmap the parquet, call cache.invalidate() and assert the PermissionError on unlink is not swallowed.

verdict.evidence: Repro at review/02-findings/repro/execution__dataframe-cache-artifact-unlink-vs-late-finalize.py reproduces the cache-PRIMITIVE property (HAZARD-1 reproduced=True: after `del lf_a; gc.collect()` then evicting A, `derived.collect()` raised `FileNotFoundError ... cache1/...parquet`), but this requires a `del` of the cache-backed scan LazyFrame that the ENGINE never performs before the derived plan is collected. Code trace of the named locations refutes the engine-level trigger: (a) src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:988-1007 `_release_consumed_parents` keeps cache-backed nodes alive — the ONLY `del lazy_outputs[pid]` (line 1007) is gated by `pid not in cache_backed_node_ids` (line 1005); Grep confirms exactly one `del lazy_outputs` in the file. (b) The `del lf` at line 1410 + `pl.scan_parquet(tmp)` at 1419 is inside the `not cache_materialized` PARQUET-CHECKPOINT branch (gate at lines 1363-1366), operating on a checkpoint file, mutually exclusive with the cache-materialize branch (lines 1318-1322 set cache_materialized=True and add nid to cache_backed_node_ids). So a cache artifact's scan LF is never dropped mid-plan. (c) While the source scan LF is alive, _scan_refcounts>0 keeps the key pinned: _evict_if_over_capacity skips it, and for-cause `_remove_key` (line 536) sees `had_live_scans=True` and does NOT unlink. The returned lazy_outputs dict holds the scan LFs alive through the caller's immediate collection — verified in src/haute/routes/_explore_service.py:788-800 where `explore_lf` (the cache scan) is held while `_build_frame_stats` collects. HAZARD-2 (Windows): my main repro's invalidate() with a live scan did NOT raise and did NOT unlink (file preserved because pinned: had_live_scans=True). A separate probe proved polars `scan_parquet` does NOT hold a persistent Windows lock — `Path.unlink` succeeds even after `.collect()` (`unlink raised: None`, file deleted); only a raw OS handle yields `PermissionError [WinError 32]`, which haute never holds on cache artifacts. While `path.unlink(missing_ok=True)` indeed only swallows ENOENT (so a PermissionError WOULD propagate), the scan-pin discipline plus pin-before-open ordering (lines 376-380: refcount++/pin under _lock, THEN scan_parquet) and lock-serialized validation/removal mean unlink never fires against a live polars reader.
verdict.repro_outcome: HAZARD-1 reproduced ONLY at the cache-primitive level via a manual `del lf_a; gc.collect()` the engine never does: entry_a_evicted=True, artifact_exists_after_evict=False, derived.collect() raised FileNotFoundError. HAZARD-2 NOT reproduced: invalidate() did not raise and did not unlink (file preserved because the live scan kept the key pinned). Engine-level code trace shows the keep-alive discipline prevents hazard-1's trigger from ever occurring; hence the claim's described failure is unreachable through the production execution path.

claim.title: execute_sink coerces a live sink to the first non-live live_switch scenario (or 'batch'); when no live_switch defines that exact fallback, edge pruning removes all branches into the switch and the sink fails with an opaque missing-input error rather than a clear config error
claim.location: src/haute/executor.py:1344-1367 (_resolve_batch_scenario), 1475-1478 (sink_scenario = _resolve_batch_scenario(graph) or 'batch'), then _execute_lazy prune via prepare_graph(source=sink_scenario)
claim.failure_scenario: _resolve_batch_scenario scans live_switch input_scenario_map values and returns the first non-live scenario name, raising only if two DIFFERENT non-live names appear. execute_sink then sets sink_scenario to that value, else 'batch'. Two failure modes: (a) A graph has live_switch nodes whose ISM maps inputs only to 'live' (so _resolve_batch_scenario returns None) -> sink_scenario='batch'; if those switches have no input mapped to 'batch', prune_live_switch_edges drops every edge into the switch for source='batch', and _build_lazy_node later raises ValueError('No input data available for node ...') — a confusing failure instead of a clear 'no batch branch configured' error. (b) Dict iteration of ism.values() returns the non-live scenario, but if the graph's actual batch branch uses a DIFFERENT scenario label than the one picked (e.g. two switches, one 'overnight', one only 'live'; picked='overnight' but the live-only switch has no 'overnight' input), the same all-edges-pruned ValueError surfaces. The sink_scenario also seeds the dataframe_cache_request input_fingerprint/source and the cache key, so the wrong scenario silently keys the cache under a branch the user never intended.
claim.repro_strategy: Build a graph: source -> live_switch(L) -> dataSink, where L.config.input_scenario_map maps its single input to 'live' only. Call execute_sink(graph, sink_node_id). _resolve_batch_scenario returns None -> sink_scenario='batch'; prepare_graph(source='batch') prunes the only edge into L; assert it raises ValueError about missing input for L (opaque) rather than a typed configuration error naming the missing batch branch. Variant for (b): two live_switch nodes, one ISM {in: 'overnight'}, one ISM {in: 'live'}; assert the run picks 'overnight' and the live-only switch loses all inputs.

verdict.evidence: Ran the repro driving the REAL _resolve_batch_scenario, prune_live_switch_edges, and _execute_lazy in-memory. Mode (a) [source -> live_switch{src:'live'} -> sink]: resolved_batch_scenario=None, sink_scenario='batch', edge_into_switch_survives_pruning=True, raised_type=None, collected_ok=True (3 rows). Mode (b) [switch A ISM{srcA:'overnight'}, switch B ISM{srcB:'live'}]: resolved='overnight', edge_into_A_survives_pruning=True, edge_into_B_survives_pruning=True, raised_type=None, collected_ok=True. Both 'claim_mode_X_reproduced' flags are False. No 'No input data available' error occurred in either mode. The decisive guard the finder missed is projection.py:2091 inside prune_live_switch_edges: `if source not in input_scenario_map.values(): continue` — when the resolved batch scenario ('batch' in mode a, 'overnight' for the live-only switch B in mode b) is absent from that switch's ISM values, the switch is SKIPPED for pruning and its input edges are preserved. Additionally, line 2101 only excludes edges whose `mapped != source`, so whenever a switch IS processed at least one input (the one mapped to `source`) always survives — making 'all branches pruned' structurally impossible. The live_switch builder (_builders.py:633-666) returns is_source=False and switch_fn passes its lone input through via the documented unmapped-scenario fallback (logged: live_switch_unmapped_scenario), so the sink executes normally rather than failing with an opaque missing-input error.
verdict.repro_outcome: Script ran to completion; all refutation assertions passed. Mode (a) and (b) both: input edge into the live-only switch SURVIVES pruning, execution succeeds (collected_ok=True), no ValueError('No input data available') raised. The claim's all-edges-pruned -> opaque-failure mechanism did not reproduce.

claim.title: ExecutionContext memory limit is a coarse post-hoc gate sampled only at checkpoint()/stage() boundaries; a single node's collect/sink that balloons RSS between two checkpoints is never interrupted and can OOM before any check fires
claim.location: src/haute/_execution_context.py:702-712 (checkpoint samples RSS), 863-887 (_check_memory_budget), 950-957 (_effective_rss_limit_bytes); enforcement points are only the explicit checkpoint/stage calls in _execute_lazy / _execute_eager_core / chunking
claim.failure_scenario: The bounded-memory guarantee is checkpoint-granular: _check_memory_budget runs only when checkpoint() or stage() entry/exit is invoked, sampling process RSS and raising ExecutionMemoryLimitExceededError if over the effective limit. Between two checkpoints — notably inside a single streaming_collect of one heavy node, or a single Polars operation that materialises a large intermediate (a wide join, an explode, a non-streamable plan that falls back to .collect() under allow_broad on PREVIEW_EAGER) — there is no sampling, so a node whose peak RSS spikes 10x within one collect can OOM-kill the process before the next checkpoint observes anything. Adaptive budgets are also computed from available_ram at ADMISSION time (_adaptive_default_memory_limit_bytes) and never re-derived, so a budget sized when 8GiB was free is enforced even if another process later consumes that RAM. This makes 'bounded memory' a between-stage promise, not a continuous one — relevant because the admission layer and route 400s present it as a hard cap.
claim.repro_strategy: Create an ExecutionContext with a tiny memory_limit_bytes and a memory_sampler stub that returns a value UNDER the limit at every checkpoint but would be over mid-collect. Run a single node whose collect allocates above the limit; assert no ExecutionMemoryLimitExceededError is raised during that node (the stub is only consulted at checkpoint boundaries, which all read under-limit values), demonstrating that intra-collect growth is invisible to the gate. The code-trace alone (no _check_memory_budget call inside streaming_collect) substantiates the granularity claim.

verdict.evidence: Both code-trace and executed repro confirm the claim. Code-trace: streaming_collect (src/haute/_polars_utils.py:51-92) contains NO _check_memory_budget / checkpoint call — it just runs lf.collect(engine="streaming") (line 75) or, under allow_broad on PREVIEW_EAGER, the broad lf.collect() fallback (line 92). In _execute_eager_core the collect is wrapped only as ctx.checkpoint(before_collect) / with ctx.stage("eager_collect"): streaming_collect(...) / ctx.checkpoint(after_collect) (src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:1994-2001). _check_memory_budget (src/haute/_execution_context.py:863-887) is invoked ONLY at checkpoint() (line 712), stage() entry (line 727 on rss_start) and stage() exit (line 780 on rss_end). A Grep for threads/Timer/watchdog confirmed there is NO background RSS-sampling thread; every enforcement point is an explicit checkpoint/stage boundary. The stale-budget sub-claim also holds: _adaptive_default_memory_limit_bytes (src/haute/_execution_admission.py:361-372) reads available = available_ram_bytes() once, and create_admitted_execution_context fixes rss_limit_bytes = rss_at_admission + budget.memory_limit_bytes (line 427) with no re-derivation during execution. Executed repro output: "values gate actually evaluated during node = [50, 50, 50, 50] (all <= 100)" while "intra_collect_peak_rss = 1000 (10x over limit)" and "peak 1000 was NEVER passed to _check_memory_budget -> no OOM guard"; the same value 1000 placed AT a checkpoint boundary DID raise ExecutionMemoryLimitExceededError, proving the gate works but is only boundary-granular.
verdict.repro_outcome: PASS — REPRO_OK: claim substantiated. The scripted memory_sampler is consulted only at the 4 boundary points (checkpoint entry, stage entry, stage exit, final checkpoint), all returning 50 (under the limit of 100). A 1000-byte (10x over) peak modeled inside the stage body (intra-collect growth) is never evaluated by _check_memory_budget, so no ExecutionMemoryLimitExceededError is raised across the node. Control case: the same 1000 value present at a checkpoint boundary does raise, confirming the limit is enforced but only at checkpoint/stage granularity — not continuously. The assertion targets the specific wrong behaviour (gate observed values [50,50,50,50], peak 1000 absent from observed set), not merely "something raised".
verdict.blast_radius: Bounded-memory guarantee is a between-stage promise, not continuous. The exposed window is the duration of a single node's collect/sink between two checkpoints. Realistic exploiters: the allow_broad .collect() fallback (PREVIEW_EAGER only, _polars_utils.py:92 / _execute_lazy.py:1992), or any single non-streamed materialisation that Polars internally spikes (wide join / explode / pivot) inside one streaming_collect or bounded_sink, where peak intra-op RSS can exceed the effective limit and OOM-kill the process before the after_collect checkpoint samples. Also affects every other stage()-wrapped collect (chunking.py:1025, deploy/_scorer.py:869, _train_service.py:945, _polars_utils.bounded_collect_batches per-batch). Plus stale adaptive budget: a budget sized when 8GiB was free is enforced unchanged if another process later consumes RAM. Default streaming engine keeps per-step RSS bounded, the admission process_rss_limit_bytes gate exists, and RSS is re-sampled every checkpoint, which collectively limit real-world impact and justify low severity.
verdict.recommended_fix: Continuous enforcement is the only true fix and is heavy. Lightweight option: run a daemon watchdog thread per ExecutionContext that polls memory_sampler() at a bounded interval (e.g. 50-100ms) and, on breach of _effective_rss_limit_bytes(), sets cancellation_token so the next cooperative point aborts — note this still cannot pre-empt a single in-flight Polars C++ collect, so pair it with a hard process_rss_limit_bytes via OS guard (RLIMIT_AS on POSIX / Job Object on Windows) to convert silent OOM-kill into a typed failure. Separately, re-derive the adaptive budget against live available_ram at stage boundaries (or at least record drift) so a budget sized at admission is not blindly trusted. Cheapest honest change: downgrade the docs/route-400 language from "hard cap" to "checkpoint-granular bound" so the admission layer does not over-promise. Pre-req: add failing tests (TDD per repo CLAUDE.md) asserting an intra-collect breach is detected/aborted before completion.
verdict.coordinate_risk: Yes — moderate. Current branch is wave-2-cache-integrity and the subsystem under review is the execution engine (eager/lazy/chunked + admission + concurrency). _execution_context.py, _execution_admission.py, _execute_lazy.py and _polars_utils.py are the precise hot files an in-flight execution/cache branch is most likely editing; any watchdog-thread or admission-budget change must coordinate with concurrent work on checkpoint(), stage(), the cancellation_token, and the admission reservation/release path to avoid merge conflicts and double-enforcement.

claim.title: Inline efficient-frontier compute catches every exception into a non-fatal frontier_error string while the solve is reported as fully completed
claim.location: src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:2191-2243 (_finalize_solve_result); surfaced at src/haute/routes/optimiser.py:1219-1236 (solve_status) and frontend/src/panels/OptimiserPreview.tsx:396-407
claim.failure_scenario: A solve runs with config.frontier_enabled=True and constraints set. After the primary solve succeeds, _finalize_solve_result computes the frontier inline inside a try/except Exception. Any genuine fault in the frontier sweep — infeasible threshold_ranges, solver divergence/non-convergence inside price_contour, a NaN/overflow in the predictor-corrector lambdas, or a real library bug — is caught, logged at WARNING, and written only as result['frontier_error'] = 'Frontier unavailable: <exc>'. The job still transitions to status='completed' with progress=1.0 and result['frontier']=None. The status endpoint returns status='completed' and the frontend renders the failure as a small text-xs AlertCircle warning chip beside an otherwise-successful result panel, so an actuary can easily miss that the efficient frontier they will use to pick a price point silently did not compute.
claim.repro_strategy: Build a minimal online QuoteGrid via the route (a 2-quote x 2-step long frame, one sum constraint), set config.frontier_enabled=True and frontier_ranges to an infeasible/degenerate pair that makes solver.frontier raise (or monkeypatch _compute_frontier to raise RuntimeError). POST /solve, poll /solve/status to completion, and assert that status=='completed' while result['frontier'] is None and result['frontier_error'] is a string — demonstrating a frontier failure does not fail the job, contradicting the repo's fail-loud mandate.

verdict.evidence: Reproduced by execution against the real `_finalize_solve_result`. With config={constraints:{volume:{min:0.9}}, frontier_enabled:True, frontier_ranges:{volume:{min:0.8,max:1.1}}} and a mock solver whose `.frontier(...)` raises RuntimeError('predictor-corrector diverged: lambda overflow (NaN)'), the run printed: solver.frontier called=True; job status='completed'; job progress=1.0; result['frontier']=None; result['frontier_error']='Frontier unavailable: predictor-corrector diverged: lambda overflow (NaN)'; job['frontier_data']=None. The library logged 'frontier_computation_failed' at WARNING with an exc_info traceback, then completed the job. This matches the code: src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:2191-2239 wraps the entire frontier sweep (range build + `_compute_frontier` -> `solver.frontier`) in `try/except Exception` that only sets `frontier_error = f"Frontier unavailable: {exc}"` and logs WARNING; lines 2241-2284 then unconditionally build completion_fields (progress=1.0) and call JobLifecycle(...).transition(to="completed"). Surfacing chain confirmed: schemas.py:1159 `frontier_error: str|None`; optimiser.py solve_status (1228-1237) returns status=completed with result passthrough; frontend types.ts:658 and OptimiserPreview.tsx:396-407 render it as a text-xs AlertCircle chip. COUNTER-EVIDENCE (why severity is low, not medium): the behaviour is deliberate and documented ('non-fatal' comment at _optimiser_service.py:2184), is covered by an EXISTING passing test `test_frontier_failure_is_surfaced_on_completed_status` (tests/test_optimiser_routes.py:8140-8187) which asserts exactly status=='completed' + frontier_error surfaced on /solve/status, the frontier is an opt-in secondary artifact while the primary solve genuinely succeeded, and no incorrect frontier is fabricated (frontier is explicitly None with an explicit error string). So the failure is NOT silent and NOT a value-substituting fallback; 'silently did not compute' overstates it. The real residual weakness is that status stays 'completed'/progress=1.0 so a programmatic consumer keying on status would assume a frontier is present, and the UI emphasis (small chip) is low for an artifact used to pick a price point.
verdict.repro_outcome: PASS (exit 0, "CLAIM REPRODUCED"). solver.frontier raised; job ended status='completed', progress=1.0, result['frontier']=None, result['frontier_error']='Frontier unavailable: predictor-corrector diverged: lambda overflow (NaN)'. Assertions on the specific wrong values (completed+1.0+None+non-empty error string, original exc text buried in the soft string) all held. Isolation: in-memory JobStore + tempfile project root via haute._sandbox.set_project_root; no src/tests/rating file read or written.
verdict.blast_radius: Only the optional efficient-frontier artifact on solves where frontier_enabled=True and constraints are set. The primary solve (objective, lambdas, constraints, converged) is unaffected and correct. Impact is confined to: (a) any programmatic consumer that treats status=='completed' as "frontier available" without checking result['frontier']/result['frontier_error'] (would proceed with frontier=None), and (b) an actuary who overlooks the low-emphasis warning chip and assumes the frontier price-point picker computed when it did not. No data corruption, no wrong values fabricated, no effect on apply/persisted results.
verdict.recommended_fix: Keep the solve non-fatal (the primary result is valid) but make the partial failure unmissable rather than re-architecting to hard-fail: (1) raise UI emphasis for frontier_error from a text-xs chip to a prominent inline error state on the Frontier tab (and disable/replace the frontier price-point picker when frontier is None), so the optional-artifact failure cannot be skimmed past; (2) optionally add a machine-readable signal alongside status (e.g. result['frontier_status']='failed' or a partial_failures list) so programmatic consumers cannot infer frontier presence from status=='completed'. Narrow the catch from bare `except Exception` to the specific frontier/solver exception types and let truly unexpected programming errors (e.g. TypeError/KeyError from a real bug) propagate to fail the job, consistent with the fail-loud mandate. Note an existing test (test_optimiser_routes.py:8140-8187) encodes the current contract and would need updating in lockstep.
verdict.coordinate_risk: Moderate. src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py is the optimiser god-file and a hot area; the current branch is wave-2-cache-integrity and recent commits touch the rating optimiser, so an in-flight branch could be editing nearby. The fix itself is small and localised (one try/except scope + one frontend render block + optionally one schema field), but any change must be coordinated with the existing contract test test_frontier_failure_is_surfaced_on_completed_status and the sibling missing/partial-range tests (test_optimiser_routes.py ~7835-7906, 8140-8187) which currently assert status=='completed' with frontier_error set.

claim.title: Ratebook frontier-point selection/save re-solves coordinate descent from the stored point's lambdas instead of using the sweep's recorded optimum, so saved factor tables can disagree with the displayed frontier point
claim.location: src/haute/routes/optimiser.py:846-909 (_materialise_ratebook_frontier_point) + 750-781 (_materialised_ratebook_result_dict); re-solve via .venv/Lib/site-packages/price_contour/ratebook.py:341-460 (RatebookOptimiser.solve with lambdas + _constraints_override)
claim.failure_scenario: When a user selects (or saves/MLflow-logs) a ratebook efficient-frontier point, _materialise_ratebook_frontier_point does NOT reuse the totals/factor tables the frontier sweep computed for that point. It calls solver.solve(quote_grid, factor_contexts, lambdas=point_lambdas, _constraints_override=threshold_from_point) — a fresh full coordinate-descent pass warm-started from the point's recorded lambdas — and then _materialised_ratebook_result_dict overwrites total_objective, constraints, baseline_*, and factor_tables from THIS re-solve. The frontier sweep itself (ratebook.py:690-999) reaches each point via nearest-neighbour ordering and a linear lambda predictor-corrector, i.e. a DIFFERENT warm-start trajectory. Coordinate descent on a ratebook is not guaranteed to land on a unique global optimum; two different warm-starts can converge to two different stationary points. The factor tables (the actual saved rates) and the displayed total_objective/constraints can therefore differ from the frontier chart row the user clicked, and _build_artifact_payload persists these re-solved tables into optimiser_result.json — the artifact OPTIMISER_APPLY will deploy.
claim.repro_strategy: Construct a ratebook solve whose CD landscape has multiple stationary points (a small grid with two factor columns whose levels trade off against one constraint). Run /solve with frontier_enabled, capture a frontier point's total_objective and threshold from the returned frontier payload, then POST /frontier/select for that index and compare the materialised result's total_objective/constraints/factor_tables against the frontier-point row. Assert they match; the claim is that for a non-convex case they can differ beyond cd_tolerance because the re-solve warm-start differs from the sweep's predictor-corrector path.

verdict.repro_outcome: PASS (claim reproduced). At the tightest frontier point (threshold_cost=456), the sweep recorded obj=999.444, total_cost=453.0 (feasible), seg{A=1.10,B=0.70}, lambda_cost=0.989733. haute's materialise re-solve replicated verbatim -- solver.solve(scored, factors, factor_columns=..., lambdas={'cost':0.989733}, _constraints_override={'cost':{'max':456}}) -- converged to a DIFFERENT stationary point: obj=984.054, total_cost=484.5 (VIOLATES the 456 ceiling), seg{A=0.80,B=0.80}, lambda_cost=1.31771. Divergence vs displayed row: d_obj=15.39, d_total_cost=31.5, d_factor=0.30 (seg['A'] 1.10->0.80) -- all >> cd_tolerance=1e-3. Determinism confirmed: a COLD re-solve (lambdas=None) and a REPLAY of the sweep's exact init both reproduce the displayed point (999.444/453.0) exactly, isolating warm-start-from-stored-lambdas as the sole cause.
verdict.evidence: Code trace: _materialise_ratebook_frontier_point (optimiser.py:867-873) calls solver.solve(quote_grid, factor_contexts, factor_columns=factor_columns, lambdas=result_dict["lambdas"], _constraints_override=constraints_override) -- a fresh full CD pass (ratebook.py:530-540 run_cd_pass_py with lambdas=warm-start) warm-started from the stored point's recorded converged lambdas. The frontier sweep (ratebook.py:899-963) reaches each point via NN ordering + predictor-corrector extrapolated init lambdas and stores ONLY total_objective/total_<name>/lambda_<name> -- it discards factor_tables entirely (DataFrame built at ratebook.py:972-994 has no factor columns). _materialised_ratebook_result_dict (optimiser.py:756-774) then OVERWRITES total_objective, baseline_objective, constraints, lambdas, and factor_tables from this re-solve; _build_artifact_payload (optimiser.py:1539-1542) reads solve_result.total_objective/lambdas/total_constraints from it and persists the re-solved factor_tables to the deploy artifact. NO consistency guard exists: _cached_materialised_ratebook_frontier_result (optimiser.py:734-747) only checks selected_frontier_point==index and that the cached result's lambdas equal the point lambdas (_lambda_mappings_match, 1e-9) -- it never compares the re-solved totals/constraints/tables against the displayed frontier row, so the divergence is silently accepted and (once cached) made sticky. Executed repro output: "diverged rows = [0] ... worst factor-table divergence detail: seg['A'] sweep=1.100000 resolve=0.800000 ... d_obj=15.39 d_cost=31.5 d_factor=0.30 ... CLAIM REPRODUCED". The saved/deployed seg-A relativity (0.80) is 27% below the displayed/selected one (1.10), and the saved point violates the cost ceiling the user selected (484.5 > 456) while the displayed point honoured it.
verdict.blast_radius: Ratebook efficient-frontier point selection/save/MLflow-log only (online optimiser unaffected; non-frontier ratebook solves unaffected since they don't re-solve). Triggers when the ratebook CD landscape has multiple stationary points -- realistic at active-set kinks / tight constraint thresholds where candidate ties exist (as in the repro at the tightest ceiling). When it fires, the saved optimiser_result.json factor tables (the actual deployed rates) and the displayed/selected total_objective+constraints disagree, and the deployed point can violate the user-selected constraint. Silent: chart shows one frontier point, OPTIMISER_APPLY deploys different rates. Feasible/well-separated landscapes round-trip exactly (5 of 6 points here had d=0), so it is data-dependent, not universal.
verdict.recommended_fix: Stop re-solving from the stored lambdas. Best: have the frontier sweep retain each point's authoritative factor_tables/total_objective/total_constraints (they are already computed in result at ratebook.py:937-943 -- the sweep just throws them away) and have _materialise_ratebook_frontier_point reuse the stored point's tables/totals directly instead of calling solver.solve. If a re-solve must stay (e.g. to rebuild full tables), add a loud consistency check: assert the re-solve's total_objective and each total_<name> reproduce the stored frontier row within cd_tolerance (and that the result is feasible w.r.t. the selected threshold) before persisting; on mismatch, fail loudly or retry cold (lambdas=None), which the repro shows reproduces the displayed point. The current cache (optimiser.py:734-747) only pins the wrong value once written, so it is not a fix.
verdict.coordinate_risk: Moderate. Lives in src/haute/routes/optimiser.py (a god-file) on the ratebook frontier-select/save path; current branch is wave-2-cache-integrity and recent commits touch the rating-optimiser regression/sources CI, so an in-flight branch editing optimiser frontier/cache/materialise code could collide. The fix also depends on whether price_contour.frontier is willing to surface per-point factor tables (library-side change) vs. a haute-side guard (route-only change).

claim.title: Ratebook factor levels are canonicalised at save time against the banding-source column dtype, but applied against the OPTIMISER_APPLY input column dtype; a dtype divergence for the same factor yields a silent neutral-1.0 miss
claim.location: Save: src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:1701-1761 (_canonical_ratebook_table_level) + 4660-4671 (_extract_factors, native dtypes preserved). Apply: src/haute/_builders.py:1571-1621 (_ratebook_lookup_table onMissing=neutral) joining via src/haute/_rating.py:346-370 (_rating_key_expr on the apply-input dtype)
claim.failure_scenario: At save time, level keys are canonicalised by normalise_rating_key over the BANDING-SOURCE factors frame. E.g. a Float64/Int64 factor value 25.0/25 canonicalises to '25'. At apply time, _apply_ratebook builds a rating-table lookup whose levels are those saved canonical strings, and the join applies _rating_key_expr to the OPTIMISER_APPLY INPUT frame's factor column using THAT frame's dtype. _rating_key_expr only collapses int-like floats to integer strings; a non-numeric string column is left verbatim. So if the same logical factor arrives at apply time as a Utf8 column carrying the literal label '25.0' (e.g. read from a CSV/JSON source distinct from the banding source, or after an upstream cast), the apply key is '25.0' while the saved level is '25' -> the join misses. Because _ratebook_lookup_table sets onMissing='neutral' with no defaultValue, the miss applies factor 1.0 to that quote (counted/logged, but the rate the solver actually computed is dropped). The mispricing is per-quote and only loud in logs, not in the API result.
claim.repro_strategy: Solve a ratebook with a banding source whose factor column is Float64 25.0 (saves level '25'). Then run apply (or the OPTIMISER_APPLY node) over an input frame where that factor column is Utf8 '25.0'. Assert the resulting *_optimised_factor is 1.0 (neutral miss) and rating_table_lookup_misses fired, even though level '25' exists in the saved table — demonstrating the save-vs-apply canonicalisation dtype boundary produces a silent neutral rate rather than the solved factor.

verdict.repro_outcome: PASS (bug reproduced). Save side (real _ratebook_factor_level_counts + _canonical_ratebook_table_level over a Float64 25.0 banding frame) stores canonical level '25'. CONTROL: applying that artifact to a Float64 25.0 input frame -> age_optimised_factor = 1.5 (solved factor, artifact correct). BUG: applying the SAME artifact to a Utf8 '25.0' input frame -> age_optimised_factor = 1.0 with a `rating_table_lookup_misses` warning (missing_keys=[{'age': '25.0'}]). The neutral-1.0 miss silently replaces the solved 1.5 in the API result column.
verdict.evidence: Save: src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:1663-1677 (_ratebook_factor_level_key) and 1701-1761 (_canonical_ratebook_table_level) canonicalise via normalise_rating_key against the banding-source dtype; for Float64 25.0 the saved __factor_group__ is '25' (line 2069). normalise_rating_key (_rating.py:339-343) collapses int-like floats to '25' but leaves strings verbatim ('25.0' stays '25.0', line 343). Apply: _builders.py:1571-1621 sets onMissing='neutral' with no defaultValue; _rating.py:_apply_rating_table:583+596 applies _rating_key_expr to the apply-input column on THAT frame's dtype (line 346-370: Utf8 -> verbatim cast, line 370). Saved '25' vs apply Utf8 '25.0' -> join miss -> output null -> filled 1.0 (_builders.py:1680). No guard reconciles save-vs-apply dtype: _validate_supported_factor_dtypes (_rating.py:386-388/591) only rejects Date/Datetime; the save-time collision guards (1922-1927, 2052-2057) only catch intra-frame type mixing. Repro output observed: "[save] SAVED canonical level = '25'", "[apply] Float64 25.0 input -> age_optimised_factor = 1.5", "rating_table_lookup_misses ... missing_keys=[{'age': '25.0'}]", "[apply] Utf8 '25.0' input -> age_optimised_factor = 1.0".
verdict.blast_radius: Per-quote silent mispricing on OPTIMISER_APPLY: any factor whose apply-input column dtype diverges from the banding-source dtype such that one collapses an int-like float and the other does not (Float64/Int64 25.0/25 vs Utf8 '25.0'; or Utf8 '25.0' saved vs Float64 25.0 applied). Affects only logically int-like-float factor levels; pure-string categoricals ('young') and consistently-typed factors are unaffected. Every affected quote silently rates the neutral 1.0 instead of the solved relativity. The miss IS counted/logged (rating_table_lookup_misses WARNING) and flagged 'unseen' on the explainability ladder, so it is observable in logs but not in the API result value.

claim.title: A non-integer or out-of-pattern Float scenario_index passes the finite-value contract but is silently truncated when cast to Int32, merging distinct scenario steps
claim.location: src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:4458-4479 (finite_columns includes step_col but cast_to_float32_columns excludes it; _non_finite_check_columns at 221-226 only checks float cols) and cast_map[step_col]=pl.Int32() at 4469
claim.failure_scenario: _validate_and_project lists scenario_index (step_col) in finite_columns, but _value_contract_validation_exprs only NaN/inf-checks it after a Float32 cast when step_col is in cast_to_float32_columns — and it is NOT (cast set is {objective, mult_col, *constraint_cols}). _non_finite_check_columns further restricts checks to columns whose source dtype is_float(). The grid builder then sees duplicate (quote_id, scenario_index) rows: the optimiser silently optimises over a corrupted scenario set (one step effectively shadows another) with no contract error. Integer-typed scenario_index is unaffected; the hazard is a float-typed scenario_index from an upstream expression.
claim.repro_strategy: Build a long frame where scenario_index is Float64 with values [2.0, 2.5] for a single quote_id (plus valid objective/scenario_value), POST /solve, and observe the solve succeeds (no 400 contract error) while the grid has two rows mapped to scenario_index Int32 2 — i.e. 2.5 truncated to 2 silently. Compare against integer scenario_index to show the divergence.

verdict.evidence:
Repro exercises the module's OWN validation helpers (_non_finite_check_columns, _value_contract_validation_exprs, _non_finite_detail_from_counts) plus the verbatim cast logic from _validate_and_project (src/haute/routes/_optimiser_service.py:4458-4479). Key output lines:

[A'] columns the contract actually NaN/inf-checks -> ['expected_income', 'scenario_value', 'scenario_index']  (step IS checked, yet passes -> the gap is integrality, not coverage; the check is is_nan()/is_infinite(), and 2.5 is finite)
[B] projected rows -> scenario_index: [2, 2]  (cast(pl.Int32) at line 4469 truncates 2.5 -> 2)
[B] duplicate (quote_id, scenario_index) groups after cast -> 1  (two distinct scenario steps collapsed onto one grid key for q1, no error)
[C] control: NaN objective IS rejected with a 400-detail string mentioning 'expected_income' -> the validation machinery is live, confirming the integrality hole is specific and real.
The code comment at 4450-4451 ('scenario_index is cast to Int32 downstream, so its source values are checked') is the precise false-assurance: the source IS checked, but only for finiteness, never for integrality. No upstream guard forces an integer dtype; the optimiser accepts an arbitrary data_input and a user-remappable scenario_index column (the product's own scenario expander at _builders.py:886 emits a clean Int32 range, but its post-expansion user-code hook and arbitrary upstream nodes can yield a Float64 scenario_index).
verdict.repro_outcome: EXIT=0. All assertions hold: fractional Float64 scenario_index [2.0, 2.5] passes the value contract (detail=None), is cast to Int32 [2, 2] (2.5 silently truncated), producing exactly one duplicate (quote_id, scenario_index) group; control confirms a NaN objective is still correctly rejected. claim.title: Auto-range achievable envelope sums per-quote Float32 extrema in Float32, accumulating rounding error in the frontier range bounds for large portfolios

claim.title: Duplicate top-level @pipeline function names produce two GraphNodes with the same id; executor collapses them and the first node's pricing body is silently lost
claim.location: src/haute/_ast_helpers.py:269-276 (_extract_function_bodies keys bodies by func name, later overwrites earlier); src/haute/_graph_builders.py:58-99 (_extract_decorated_nodes), 166-181 (_build_rf_nodes uses func_name as GraphNode.id); collapse at src/haute/executor.py:1327 and src/haute/codegen.py:924 (node_map = {n.id: n ...})
claim.failure_scenario: A pipeline file defines two functions with the same name, both decorated (e.g. two `@pipeline.polars def step(df)` with different bodies `pl.lit(111)` vs `pl.lit(222)`). _extract_function_bodies stores only the LAST body under key 'step', so _extract_decorated_nodes attaches `pl.lit(222)` to BOTH raw nodes; _build_rf_nodes emits two GraphNodes both with id='step'. The executor builds `node_map = {n.id: n for n in graph.nodes}` which collapses the two to a single 'step' node carrying `pl.lit(222)` -> the first node's logic (`pl.lit(111)`) never executes and never appears. codegen._error_on_name_collisions explicitly does NOT flag two nodes with the *identical* label (it only flags distinct labels colliding after sanitisation), so there is no loud error anywhere; the wrong-but-valid graph executes and round-trips. Verified by repro: parsed node ids ['step','step'], both bodies == pl.lit(222), executor node_map keys == ['step'].
claim.repro_strategy: parse_pipeline_source of a 4-line file with two `@pipeline.polars def step(df)` defs with distinct bodies; assert len({n.id for n in g.nodes}) == 1 while len(g.nodes) == 2, and that both g.nodes[i].data.config['code'] equal the SECOND body.

verdict.evidence: Executed repro on synthetic 2x `@pipeline.polars def step(raw)` source (bodies pl.lit(111) vs pl.lit(222)). Output: `all node ids : ['step', 'step']`; `step codes : ['def step(raw): return raw.with_columns(marker=pl.lit(222))', 'def step(raw): return raw.with_columns(marker=pl.lit(222))']` — BOTH nodes carry the SECOND body; the first body (111) is absent from the graph entirely (silently lost). `executor node_map keys : ['step']` — the {n.id: n for n in graph.nodes} idiom (executor.py:1327, codegen.py:924) collapses the two physical nodes to one. All four assertions in the repro passed (script exit 0). Root cause confirmed in source: _ast_helpers.py:269-274 keys `bodies[node.name]` so the later `step` overwrites the earlier; _graph_builders.py:170 sets GraphNode.id = n['func_name'] yielding two id='step' nodes. codegen.py:569-576 `_error_on_name_collisions` only flags buckets where `len(set(originals)) > 1`, so two identical 'step' labels (set == {'step'}, len 1) are NOT flagged — confirmed by the repro raising no sanitize-collision ParseError. No duplicate-node-id guard exists in PipelineGraph schema or validate_pipeline_graph_shape_contracts (_graph_shape.py:65 validates edge/handle shape only). Nuance: in the specific 2-node shapes I tried, the shared id made the implicit/fallback edges self-referential and codegen's downstream cycle check raised CycleError — so the *codegen* path is sometimes (not reliably) caught by an unrelated error, but the *executor* node_map collapse is a bare dict-comprehension with no guard and is genuinely silent; the first node's body never executes.
verdict.repro_outcome: PASS (exit 0) — reproduced. Printed: node ids ['step','step']; both config['code'] == pl.lit(222) body; '111' absent from both; executor node_map keys ['step']; no sanitize-collision ParseError raised by codegen (it raised an unrelated CycleError for this particular graph shape, which the repro correctly distinguished from the name-collision error the claim is about).
verdict.blast_radius: Any pipeline file (hand-authored or AI-generated) that accidentally defines two top-level decorated functions with the same name. The earlier function's entire pricing/transform body is dropped at parse time with no error, no warning, and no GUI surfacing; the round-tripped graph carries only the last body. Affects parser.parse_pipeline_source and every consumer of the resulting graph (executor, codegen, projection, GUI). In practice the most-impacted real path is the GUI/save path where the parsed graph is the source of truth — a duplicate-name typo silently deletes a node's logic on the next save. The executor itself loses the first node's outputs whenever two same-id nodes survive into execution. Mitigating factor that lowers severity from 'high' to 'medium': with the minimal 2-node arrangements the shared id tends to create a self/back edge that codegen's cycle detector catches (a loud, if misleading, CycleError), so the *fully silent disk-corruption* round-trip requires a graph shape where the duplicate nodes do not form a cycle; the silent body-loss at parse time, however, is unconditional.
verdict.recommended_fix: Detect duplicate node ids (== duplicate decorated function names) loudly at parse time, where the data actually collides, rather than relying on the label-sanitization collision check that intentionally skips identical labels. Two viable spots: (1) In _ast_helpers._extract_function_bodies, detect a second `node.name` already present in `bodies` for a *decorated* function and raise ParseError naming the function and both line numbers; or (2) add an explicit duplicate-id guard in parser.parse_pipeline_source / _build_rf_nodes after raw_nodes are built: `if len({n['func_name'] for n in raw_nodes}) != len(raw_nodes): raise ParseError(...)`. Also tighten codegen._error_on_name_collisions so two nodes with the *identical* label are flagged too (the current comment 'the executor handles elsewhere' is false — the executor's node_map silently drops one). Add a failing test: parse source with two `@pipeline.polars def step(df)` distinct bodies and assert ParseError is raised (per CLAUDE.md TDD: write the failing test first).
verdict.coordinate_risk: Low-to-moderate. The fix touches src/haute/_ast_helpers.py, src/haute/_graph_builders.py, src/haute/parser.py, and src/haute/codegen.py (_error_on_name_collisions). The current branch is wave-2-cache-integrity (cache/execution focus) which does not appear to edit the parser/codegen name-collision logic, so direct conflict is unlikely. However codegen._error_on_name_collisions and the parser are hot, widely-depended-on areas; any change to collision semantics should run the full parser/codegen/round-trip test suite to avoid regressing the existing 'distinct labels collide' behavior. The _api_input_schema.py v2 path already has its own label-collision check (B2) and should be cross-checked for consistency.

claim.title: Trace expression evaluator returns wrong/None values vs real Polars for horizontal funcs and unsupported functions, shown as the computed price-explanation value

claim.title: Expression parse/evaluate/compute/chain wrap everything in `except Exception` and fall back to the raw row value, masking evaluator bugs as self-consistent waterfalls
claim.location: src/haute/_expression_parser.py:993-1003 (parse_expression), 1302-1325 (evaluate_expression -> result_value=row_values.get(target)), 1536-1539 (_compute_result -> row_values.get(target)), 2149-2156 (parse_expression_chain)
claim.failure_scenario: Every public entry point of the trace expression engine has a top-level `except Exception` that converts ANY internal failure (AttributeError/TypeError/KeyError from a malformed AST shape, an unsupported construct, a real bug in a dispatch method) into either an 'opaque' ParsedExpression or, in evaluate_expression/_compute_result, a fall-through to `row_values.get(target_column)` — i.e. the evaluator returns the ALREADY-OBSERVED value as if it had computed it. Because the 'computed' step then equals the observed value, the waterfall reconciles and looks correct, so the bug is invisible in the UI and in tests that compare the evaluator against its own output. This is the exact 'broad try/except hides a wrong number' pattern the architecture map flags and CLAUDE.md forbids; it allows the horizontal-func divergences above (and future regressions) to go permanently unnoticed.
claim.repro_strategy: Monkeypatch or feed an input that throws inside _compute_result_impl (e.g. a node code referencing an unsupported call that raises) and assert evaluate_expression returns result_value == row_values[target] with no exception/log, demonstrating the silent swallow rather than a loud failure.

verdict.evidence: Repro `review/02-findings/repro/parser__expr-evaluator-catchall-masks-bugs.py` ran green (uv run python). Key output lines: (A) `operator.truediv(1.0, 0.0) raises ZeroDivisionError inside _compute_result_impl` — a REAL internal evaluator failure on a perfectly valid Polars expr `pl.col('a')/pl.col('b')`; (A) `_compute_result returned -999.0 == observed row_values['ratio']` and `evaluate_expression.result_value = -999.0 == observed (-999.0)` while the correct Polars value is +inf — i.e. the catch-all at src/haute/_expression_parser.py:1536-1539 (`except Exception: return row_values.get(target_column)`) laundered the failure into the ALREADY-OBSERVED value, a demonstrably WRONG number, with no exception/log. (B) `round('abc', 2)` TypeError on `pl.col('label').round(2)` is masked identically to the observed value, showing the mask is general across dispatch methods, not one op. (C) when the target key is absent the fallback degrades to None, confirming the fallback is literally `row_values.get(target)` which launders the observed value precisely when one exists. CODE-TRACE of the caller confirms the "self-consistent waterfall" precondition AND that the inner catch-all defeats the only loud-error path: src/haute/_trace_enrichment.py:1516-1549 calls `evaluate_expression(code, column, {**step.input_values, **step.output_values}, ...)` — `step.output_values[column]` is the observed pipeline value, so `row_values[target]` is present in production. The caller wraps the call in `try/except` (1533) that would write `step.calculation={"error": ...}` on failure — but it never fires, because evaluate_expression's own `except Exception` (1302-1325) returns a well-formed EvaluatedExpression with `result_value=row_values.get(target_column)`; the caller sees `evaluated is not None`, builds a clean calc_dict, and the error marker is never written. This is exactly the "broad try/except hides a wrong number" pattern CLAUDE.md forbids ("code should be allowed to fail loudly ... far superior to a fallback which is incorrect and hard to notice").
verdict.repro_outcome: Executed successfully; all 7 assertions PASS, each asserting the predicted masking condition. Real evaluator failures (ZeroDivisionError from float division-by-zero; TypeError from round on a str) are swallowed by `_compute_result`/`evaluate_expression` and reported as `result_value` == the observed target value (-999.0 sentinel and 'untouched-observed'), which differs from the correct Polars semantics (+inf). Demonstrates a wrong VALUE, not merely that something raised.
verdict.blast_radius: Trace/explainability enrichment only (the "waterfall" UI that explains how each rated column was computed), via every public entry point of the expression engine: parse_expression (993-1003 → opaque), evaluate_expression (1302-1325), _compute_result (1536-1539), parse_expression_chain (2149-2156), plus the chain-entry fallback at _trace_enrichment.py:1572-1585. Does NOT corrupt actual rating outputs — the real pipeline computes values independently; this only fabricates the *explanation* of them. Impact: any evaluator bug or unsupported construct (a malformed/uncovered AST shape, a dispatch method raising, division-by-zero, type errors) makes the "computed" step silently equal the observed value, so the waterfall always reconciles and the divergence/regression is invisible in the UI and in any test that compares the evaluator against its own output. Masks the horizontal-func divergences referenced in the finding and any future regressions.
verdict.recommended_fix: Remove the value-laundering fallbacks and let failures surface to the caller, which already has a loud-error path. Concretely: in _compute_result (1536-1539) do not return `row_values.get(target_column)` on arbitrary exceptions — instead propagate, or return an explicit sentinel/raise a typed error (e.g. ExpressionEvaluationError) so result_value is NEVER silently set to the observed value. Likewise narrow/remove the top-level `except Exception` in evaluate_expression (1302-1325): on real failure, either re-raise (the enrichment caller at _trace_enrichment.py:1533 already converts exceptions into a visible `{"error": ...}` calculation marker) or return result_value=None with an explicit error/uncomputed flag, never `row_values.get(target_column)`. Keep parse_expression's SyntaxError→opaque path (that is legitimate user input handling) but distinguish it from internal evaluator bugs (AttributeError/TypeError/KeyError/ZeroDivisionError) which should fail loudly. Add a regression test that feeds a construct raising inside the evaluator and asserts the trace surfaces an error/None rather than silently echoing the observed value (the project's stated TDD bug workflow).
verdict.coordinate_risk: Low overlap with the in-flight branch: current branch is wave-2-cache-integrity (cache subsystem); this lives in src/haute/_expression_parser.py and src/haute/_trace_enrichment.py (Parser & DSL / trace enrichment). However the trace expression engine is a hot, heavily-tested area (recent commits touch projection/rating-optimiser regression tests), so a fix must preserve the existing loud-error contract at _trace_enrichment.py:1533/1572 and update any tests that currently assert result_value equals the observed value (which would have been passing precisely because of the mask).

claim.title: Preamble extraction over-captures the pipeline construction line when haute is imported under an alias, duplicating it on round-trip
claim.location: src/haute/_ast_helpers.py:459 (_STANDARD_IMPORTS hard-codes 'import haute'), 462-508 (_extract_preamble line/string heuristics; pipeline-start detector at 484-487 requires literal 'pipeline =' + 'haute.Pipeline')
claim.failure_scenario: A user writes `import haute as ht` and `pipeline = ht.Pipeline('p')`. _extract_preamble's standard-import sentinel set is `{'import polars as pl','import haute'}`, so the aliased import never advances `last_standard_idx` past the polars line, and the pipeline-start detector matches only `haute.Pipeline` (not `ht.Pipeline`). The captured preamble therefore runs from after `import polars as pl` through the construction line and INCLUDES `import haute as ht` and `pipeline = ht.Pipeline('p')`. Since codegen re-emits its own canonical `pipeline = haute.Pipeline(...)` and emits the preamble verbatim, the saved file gets a DUPLICATED pipeline construction (and a duplicated/aliased import) — round-trip corruption. Verified by repro: captured preamble contains `pipeline = ht.Pipeline("p")`.
claim.repro_strategy: _extract_preamble on a source using `import haute as ht` + `pipeline = ht.Pipeline('p')` between imports and the first decorator; assert the returned preamble string contains 'pipeline = ht.Pipeline', i.e. the construction line was wrongly swept into the preamble.

verdict.evidence: Executed review/02-findings/repro/parser__preamble-overcapture-aliased-import.py. For source `import polars as pl / import haute as ht / pipeline = ht.Pipeline('p') / @pipeline.polars ...`, `_extract_preamble` returns exactly "import haute as ht\n\npipeline = ht.Pipeline('p')" — i.e. it over-captures BOTH the aliased import and the construction line. Root cause confirmed in src/haute/_ast_helpers.py: `_STANDARD_IMPORTS = {"import polars as pl","import haute"}` (line 459) has no alias entry, so the start sentinel (472-475) only advances to the polars line, and the end detector (484-487) requires the literal substring `haute.Pipeline`, which `ht.Pipeline(...)` lacks. No guard elsewhere filters this: parser's `_extract_meta` (407-441) correctly reads `ht.Pipeline('p')` (target named `pipeline`, value is a Call) so the file parses and pipeline_name='p', but the over-captured preamble flows straight into codegen. A full parse->graph_to_code round-trip yields a saved file containing `Pipeline(` twice: a dead `pipeline = ht.Pipeline('p')` (verbatim from preamble, codegen.py:719) plus the canonical `pipeline = haute.Pipeline("p", description='')` (codegen.py:722), plus a redundant `import haute as ht` alongside the canonical `import haute`. So the construction line and import are DUPLICATED on round-trip, violating the documented "re-saving is a fixpoint" invariant.
verdict.repro_outcome: PASS (bug reproduced). Output: captured preamble = "import haute as ht\n\npipeline = ht.Pipeline('p')"; construction line captured: True; aliased import captured: True; regenerated source 'Pipeline(' occurrences: 2; both assertions (>=2 ctor count and verbatim aliased line present) hold. A second-cycle check shows the duplication is STABLE (gen2 == gen1, count stays 2) and the output is valid Python that still runs — so it is bounded round-trip drift, not unbounded growth or node loss.
verdict.blast_radius: Any GUI/parse->codegen save of a user pipeline file that imports haute under an alias (`import haute as ht`) and constructs via the alias. On first save the user's file silently gains a dead duplicate `pipeline = <alias>.Pipeline(...)` line and a redundant `import haute as ht`. Impact is cosmetic-but-real: confusing dead code injected into the user's source, breaking the round-trip fixpoint guarantee. NOT data loss — no nodes/edges are dropped, the canonical assignment wins at runtime, and the duplication does not accumulate across further saves. The "silent node loss" subsystem label overstates it; severity is correctly low. (Also note: a separate alias edge — `import polars as <alias>` other than `pl` — would make the start sentinel never match and return an empty preamble, dropping real preamble code; not exercised here but same root cause.)
verdict.recommended_fix: Make preamble boundary detection alias-aware, ideally AST-derived since the module already parses. From the AST, find the names haute and polars are bound to (handle `import haute`, `import haute as ht`, `import polars as pl/as X`), then (a) treat the haute import line as part of the standard-import region regardless of alias, and (b) make the pipeline-start detector match `<haute_alias>.Pipeline` (the module's actual haute binding) rather than the literal `haute.Pipeline`. A minimal string-only patch would also work: extend the start scan to also stop on any `import haute as <name>` / `import polars as <name>` line, and change the end-detector test from `"haute.Pipeline" in stripped` to a regex like `\.Pipeline(` on a `pipeline =` line. Add regression tests for both the construction-line capture and the empty-preamble polars-alias case.
verdict.coordinate_risk: Moderate. src/haute/_ast_helpers.py (_extract_preamble) and src/haute/codegen.py (_generate_pipeline_lines header) sit in the parser/codegen round-trip hot path that is under active churn on round-trip fixpoint safety (recent commits: d07f1f09 "Reject nonliteral parser inputs loudly", d216be87 "a parse gate before every write"). A fix here should coordinate with any in-flight parser/codegen work and the region-map's "re-saving is a fixpoint" invariant to avoid conflicts; current branch is wave-2-cache-integrity (cache-focused), so direct collision risk on this exact code is low right now.

claim.title: A pipeline.submodel(...) call inside a submodel file is silently ignored (nested submodels unsupported with no error)

claim.title: Training metrics use predict_proba[:,1] but scored 'prediction' column is the hard class label
claim.location: src/haute/modelling/_algorithms.py:608-615 (CatBoostAlgorithm.predict); src/haute/_mlflow_io.py:351-354 (ScoringModel.predict) and src/haute/_model_scorer.py:585-593 (_score_eager_unified)
claim.failure_scenario: Train a CatBoost classifier (task='classification'). During _compute_metrics, algo.predict(model, diag_df, features) calls model.predict_proba(x_data)[:,1], so y_pred is the positive-class PROBABILITY. compute_residuals_histogram and compute_actual_vs_predicted then compute residuals/AvE as (label - probability). At score time, ScoringModel.predict / _score_eager_unified call model.predict(x_data), which returns the HARD class label (0/1), written to the 'prediction' output column; only '<col>_proba' carries the probability. The same model therefore reports a 'prediction' with two different meanings: probability inside training diagnostics (residuals_histogram, actual_vs_predicted), hard label in the deployed/scored output. gini/auc are unaffected (rank-equivalent), but residual-style diagnostics and any consumer equating training-time predictions with scored predictions are silently inconsistent.
claim.repro_strategy: Tiny binary-classification DataFrame (2-3 numeric features, 0/1 target). Run TrainingJob(task='classification'), inspect TrainResult.actual_vs_predicted / residuals_histogram (values reflect probabilities). Then score the same rows via ModelScorer/score_frame and observe the 'prediction' column is integer labels {0,1} while '<col>_proba' holds the probabilities used in diagnostics.

verdict.evidence: Executed repro through the real production functions. Key output: train-metrics `CatBoostAlgorithm.predict` returned `[0.6031, 0.3774, 0.7802, ...]` and equaled `predict_proba[:,1]` exactly (max|train_pred - raw_proba| = 0.0); score-path `_wrap_catboost(model).predict` returned `[1, 0, 1, ...]` and equaled `model.predict()` hard labels exactly (max|score_pred - raw_label| = 0.0); the positive-class probability appeared only via `_predict_positive_proba` (the `<col>_proba` column). The two `prediction` surfaces diverge by up to 0.4985 for the same model+rows. `compute_residuals_histogram` stats['mean'] = 0.001942 exactly equaled `mean(label - probability)` (not label - label), and `compute_actual_vs_predicted`'s 'predicted' values were continuous probabilities. Code trace confirms no guard: _training_job.py:1136 `y_pred = algo.predict(...)` feeds lines 1217-1218 (residuals_histogram, actual_vs_predicted) with no classification-specific override to hard labels; _algorithms.py:610-611 returns `predict_proba(x)[:,1]` for CatBoostClassifier; _mlflow_io.py:351-354 ScoringModel.predict returns `model.predict(x)`; _model_scorer.py:585-593 writes `model.predict(...)` to output_col and routes proba separately to `<col>_proba`.
verdict.repro_outcome: PASS (all assertions held). The same CatBoost classifier yields a 'prediction' that is a positive-class PROBABILITY inside training diagnostics (residuals_histogram, actual_vs_predicted) but the HARD class LABEL {0,1} in the scored/deployed output column; the probability is only available in '<col>_proba' at score time. Confirms the claimed semantic mismatch with demonstrably divergent values (max divergence 0.4985), not an import/setup error.
verdict.blast_radius: All CatBoost classification models (task='classification'). Affected: TrainResult.residuals_histogram, residuals_stats, actual_vs_predicted, double_lift, ave_per_feature, lorenz — all computed in _compute_metrics from the probability-valued y_pred, while ModelScorer/score_frame deployed output writes the hard label to the 'prediction' column (probability only in '<col>_proba'). Ranking metrics (gini/auc/lift) are unaffected because predict_proba[:,1] is a monotonic transform of the decision function, so rank order is identical to hard-label thresholding — the claim's qualifier is correct. The concrete harm is the semantic inconsistency of the 'prediction' column between training diagnostics and scored output, affecting any consumer (UI, reconciliation, downstream join) that equates training-time predictions with scored predictions. No crash, no data corruption.
verdict.recommended_fix: Make the 'prediction' semantics consistent across training and scoring. Cleanest option: at score time for classification, write the positive-class probability to the primary 'prediction' column (matching the training diagnostics and what gini/auc/calibration consume) and, if a hard label is needed, expose it as an explicit derived column (e.g. '<col>_label'); OR conversely, leave scored 'prediction' as the probability and stop calling it a 'class label'. If hard-label output must remain the deployed 'prediction', then change CatBoostAlgorithm.predict (or the diagnostics call site) so residuals_histogram/actual_vs_predicted are computed on the same hard-label surface used at score time — but the probability is the more defensible diagnostic for calibration, so aligning scored output to the probability is preferred. Either way, document and test the invariant that training-time y_pred and scored 'prediction' carry identical semantics for a given task.
