(2) In infer_output_schema (_schema.py:134-139, called from _config.py:575) thread the same resolved artifacts through and pass them to score_graph. This routes validation through the modelScore intercept so it loads the pinned bytes AND runs _assert_runtime_contract_matches -- identical to serve. Add a regression test asserting that score_test_quotes raises FeatureMismatchError when the bundled contract drifts from a test quote (the repro is a ready template). Note: collect_artifacts must run before infer_output_schema (it already does at _config.py:571 vs 575), and the artifact dict keys already use the '{node}__{filename}' scheme the scorer expects.
verdict.coordinate_risk: Low-to-moderate. The divergent call sites (src/haute/deploy/_validators.py, _schema.py, _config.py:571-575) are the deploy-validation wiring and are not the focus of the current wave-2-cache-integrity branch. That branch touches the scorer's stat-gated artifact caches / _resolve_artifact_local (cache-integrity), which is adjacent (same _scorer.py file, and the fix routes validation through the cached load path) but the actual edit lives in the validators/schema/config modules. Coordinate by confirming the fix's added score_graph(artifact_paths=...) call interacts cleanly with any in-flight changes to the stat-gated model/contract caches. Separately noted (not part of this finding): score_graph_lazy's `except BaseException` at _scorer.py:829 cleans temp paths but does NOT release the execution_context admission on a build-time failure, leaking in-flight budget reservations -- surfaced incidentally while building the repro; worth a follow-up.

claim.title: infer_output_schema cache key (graph_fingerprint) excludes model-artifact bytes/version, so a stale output schema can be baked into the MLflow ModelSignature / manifest
claim.location: src/haute/deploy/_schema.py:95-150 (fp = graph_fingerprint(graph, output_node_id, *input_node_ids); cache read at 99-106, write at 144-148); src/haute/_cache.py:400-437 (graph_fingerprint hashes only base structural fingerprint + preamble + utility module content)
claim.failure_scenario: graph_fingerprint mixes in only node configs + edge topology + preamble text + imported utility-module source. It does NOT hash any model artifact content or the resolved MLflow version. A modelScore node configured by run_id/registered_model (version='latest' or an artifact retrained in place) keeps an identical fingerprint when the underlying model changes. infer_output_schema caches the dry-run output schema in .haute_cache/output_schema.json keyed by that fingerprint, so after a model swap that changes an output dtype (e.g. regression->classification label dtype, or an added/renamed prediction column) the stale cached schema is reused and written into the deploy manifest + MLflow ModelSignature. The deployed endpoint then advertises and validates against a contract that disagrees with reality. (Compounded by cache_path = Path('.haute_cache/output_schema.json') being CWD-relative, so the cache can also be shared/stale across projects run from the same CWD.)
claim.repro_strategy: Call infer_output_schema on a pruned graph whose output dtype depends on a modelScore artifact; capture the written .haute_cache/output_schema.json. Replace the model artifact bytes (same path) with one yielding a different output dtype WITHOUT editing any node config, call infer_output_schema again, and assert it returns the cached (stale) schema (cache_hit log) rather than re-running. Confirm graph_fingerprint(graph, out, *ins) is byte-identical across the swap.

verdict.evidence:
Confirmed by both code-trace and an executed repro that asserts on the wrong value.

CODE TRACE:
- _graph_base_fingerprint (src/haute/_cache.py:191-218) hashes ONLY per-node `id|nodeType|canonical_json(config)` (via _node_config_for_execution_fingerprint @221-227) plus edge wiring [source,sourceHandle,target,targetHandle]. graph_fingerprint (src/haute/_cache.py:400-437) additionally mixes in preamble text + imported `utility` module source — and nothing else. No model-artifact bytes, no resolved MLflow run_id/version.
- infer_output_schema (src/haute/deploy/_schema.py:95-150) computes `fp = graph_fingerprint(graph, output_node_id, *input_node_ids)` and reads .haute_cache/output_schema.json; the cache-hit branch (lines 99-106) returns `dict(cached["schema"])` and SKIPS the score_graph dry-run (line 108-150) entirely.
- modelScore models are loaded at RUNTIME from MLflow: ModelScorer._load_scoring_model_uncached -> load_mlflow_model(source_type, run_id, registered_model, version, ...) (src/haute/_model_scorer.py:1059-1070). For sourceType="registered" version="latest" the resolved version is a moving target.
- The deploy bundler (src/haute/deploy/_bundler.py:70-103, _resolve_registered_model @245-292) resolves "latest" to a concrete run only LOCALLY to download the artifact; it patches config["artifact_path"] to a constant BASENAME (line 101) but never writes the resolved run_id/version back into config. So after a "latest" retrain the node config — and thus the fingerprint — is byte-identical. (sourceType="run" with an in-place artifact retrain leaves config 100% unchanged — an even cleaner instance.)
- The inferred output_schema is baked into the MLflow ModelSignature (src/haute/deploy/_mlflow.py:249-250) and the deploy manifest (src/haute/deploy/_utils.py:52 -> consumed at src/haute/deploy/_container.py:301). The deploy flow NEVER invalidates the schema cache (the only rmtree calls target build_dir, _mlflow.py:171 / _container.py:166). Cache path Path(".haute_cache/output_schema.json") is CWD-relative, confirming the cross-project staleness sub-claim. No guard test exists — tests/test_deploy_internals.py::test_cache_hit (481-528) explicitly endorses the fingerprint-keyed short-circuit and never exercises a model-artifact swap.

EXECUTED REPRO (exit 0 = reproduced):
- [A] fingerprint (config-only) = v5:2c32d40df5bfbde9; after model 'swap' = v5:2c32d40df5bfbde9; "byte-identical across model swap: True". A config edit (output_column rename) correctly moves it to v5:fc4ef..., proving the fingerprint is a pure function of config only.
- [B] log line "output_schema_cache_hit ... fingerprint=v5:2c32d"; "dry-run (score_graph) invoked : False"; schema returned = {'Area':'String','prediction':'Float64'} (the STALE regression schema) while the swapped classification model's truthful schema is {'Area':'String','prediction':'Int64'}. score_graph was monkeypatched to raise-on-call and was never invoked, proving the cache short-circuits before any re-evaluation that would observe the new dtype.
verdict.repro_outcome: PASS (exit 0). PART A: graph_fingerprint(graph, out, in) byte-identical (v5:2c32d40df5bfbde9) across a simulated model-artifact swap with unchanged config, while an unrelated config edit moves it — proving the fingerprint excludes model content. PART B: with a cache entry seeded under that fingerprint holding a stale {'prediction':'Float64'} schema, infer_output_schema logged output_schema_cache_hit, returned the stale schema, and never invoked the score_graph dry-run (patched to raise) — so the new model's true {'prediction':'Int64'} dtype is never observed. Assertions on the exact wrong value passed.
verdict.blast_radius: Any redeploy of a pipeline whose output dtype/columns depend on a modelScore (or optimiserApply) artifact that changed without a config edit: registered_model version="latest" retrained/re-registered, OR an artifact retrained in place under a fixed run_id. The stale schema is written into both the MLflow ModelSignature and the deploy manifest (consumed by the container entrypoint), so the live endpoint advertises and validates against a contract that disagrees with the model's real output — silent wrong-contract: downstream consumers parse the wrong dtype, or MLflow signature enforcement rejects/ coerces valid responses. CWD-relative cache path additionally lets the stale entry leak across projects deployed from the same working directory. Requires a pre-existing .haute_cache/output_schema.json (created by any prior deploy/resolve from that CWD) to trigger; a clean checkout recomputes correctly.
verdict.recommended_fix: Mix model-artifact identity into the output-schema cache key (or drop the cache for graphs containing modelScore/optimiserApply nodes). Concretely: in infer_output_schema, after artifacts are resolved, fold a stat-gated fingerprint of each bundled/resolved artifact path (reuse haute.execution._stat_gated_runtime_path_fingerprint, already used at src/haute/deploy/_scorer.py:199-209) and the RESOLVED MLflow version/run_id into the cache key alongside graph_fingerprint — so "latest" moving or bytes changing invalidates the entry. Resolve relative to project root via haute._sandbox, not CWD, to stop cross-project bleed. Add a TDD regression test that seeds the cache, swaps the artifact bytes/version (mocking load_mlflow_model to flip the output dtype) without editing config, and asserts the recomputed schema (not the stale one) is returned.
verdict.coordinate_risk: High — this sits squarely in the cache-integrity surface the current branch is named for (wave-2-cache-integrity). graph_fingerprint/_cache.py and the deploy schema cache are exactly what an in-flight cache-integrity wave would be editing; coordinate so the fix lands once and the new key derivation stays consistent with any concurrent ALGO_VERSION bump or fingerprint-input changes.

claim.title: liveSwitch deploy pruning fallback (no input_scenario_map) selects the live branch by sanitized source label and does NOT raise on no-match/collision, unlike the mapped path
claim.location: src/haute/deploy/_pruner.py:46-69 (_live_only_edges: mapped path raises at 65-69 on no match; fallback path 46-57 silently leaves switch_live_source unset or matches a colliding sanitized label without any guard)
claim.failure_scenario: For a liveSwitch node whose config lacks input_scenario_map, the fallback uses inputs[0] as the live name and matches it against incoming edges by _sanitize_func_name(source.label). Two distinct upstream nodes whose labels sanitize to the same identifier (e.g. 'Live Source' and 'live_source', or 'A-B' and 'A B') both match; the first edge iterated wins, which may be the wrong branch. If the wrong upstream is selected the deployed scoring path silently feeds a different source frame than the canvas/live intent. Worse, if inputs[0] matches NO edge (renamed label) the switch keeps zero input edges (switch_live_source[sid] never set) and the node is pruned to a source with no parents — a quiet divergence rather than the loud ValueError the mapped path raises. This is a dev-vs-deploy pricing divergence with no error.
claim.repro_strategy: Construct a graph with a liveSwitch node, config with inputs=['live_source'] and NO input_scenario_map, and two upstream source nodes with labels 'live source' and 'Live-Source' both sanitizing to 'live_source', wired to the switch. Call prune_for_deploy and assert which source edge survives is order-dependent / wrong; separately set inputs=['renamed'] matching no edge and assert prune_for_deploy silently drops all switch inputs (no ValueError) versus the mapped path which raises.

verdict.repro_outcome: see above
verdict.evidence: The cited asymmetry is literally present (deploy/_pruner.py: mapped path raises at 65-69 on no-match; fallback 46-57 silently leaves switch_live_source[sid] unset / picks first colliding edge with no guard), and my executed repro demonstrates both order-dependent selection and silent zero-input pruning vs the mapped ValueError. HOWEVER the claim's production failure narrative ("deployed scoring path silently feeds a different source frame than canvas/live intent") is REFUTED by an upstream invariant the finder missed: prune_for_deploy has exactly ONE production caller (deploy/_config.py:551), fed by parse_pipeline_file (deploy/_config.py:543). In a parsed graph, _graph_builders.py:170-174 sets BOTH node id and data.label to func_name (a valid Python identifier) with no label-override path. _sanitize_func_name is the identity on identifiers (verified: 'Live_Source'->'Live_Source', etc.) and injective on distinct identifiers, so (A) two distinct upstream func_names can NEVER sanitize-collide — the collision is structurally impossible on the deploy path. For (B), the switch's config inputs = param_names (_config_builder.py:108) and codegen sets the switch params to exactly the wired source_names (_codegen_builders.py:524), so inputs[0] always corresponds to a wired source whose label==func_name==inputs[0]; a no-match requires a hand-broken module with a dangling first param, which has no live branch to keep anyway. Thus the repro's divergence only manifests with synthetic free-form labels that the production parser never produces. The asymmetry is a genuine but latent robustness gap, not the claimed medium-severity dev-vs-deploy pricing divergence.

claim.title: collect_artifacts rewrites config['artifact_path'] = basename in place on the shared node config dict, making bundling non-idempotent and leaking the shortened path
claim.location: src/haute/deploy/_bundler.py:95-104 (config["artifact_path"] = Path(artifact_path).name; artifact_name = f"{nid}__{config['artifact_path']}")
claim.failure_scenario: In the MODEL_SCORE branch the bundler mutates the live node's config dict (`config = node.data.config`) by overwriting `artifact_path` with just the basename. pruned_graph is a model_copy of the full graph, but GraphNode.data.config is a shared dict object (Pydantic model_copy is shallow), so this in-place patch alters the original full graph's node config too, and the manifest's pruned_graph (serialized later) now carries a basename-only artifact_path. A second call to collect_artifacts on the same graph object computes the artifact key from the already-shortened path (Path(basename).name == basename), so the key is stable here, but any other consumer that re-resolves config['artifact_path'] as a real path (e.g. re-running resolve_config, or the scorer's _remap_artifact which keys on `{nid}__{Path(raw_path).name}`) now sees a different value than the pristine config. The mutation also means resolve_config is not safely re-runnable on the same in-memory graph. This is silent shared-state mutation across the full/pruned graph boundary.
claim.repro_strategy: Build a graph with a modelScore node config artifact_path='models/deep/model.cbm' and run collect_artifacts (mock _download_model_artifact). Assert the ORIGINAL graph node's config['artifact_path'] changed to 'model.cbm' (proving in-place mutation of shared dict), and that calling collect_artifacts twice on the same graph object produces differing intermediate state / depends on call order.

verdict.evidence: Executed review/02-findings/repro/platform__deploy-bundler-mutates-shared-node-config-in-place.py. The FACTUAL premise reproduces: prune_for_deploy keeps the same GraphNode objects (kept_nodes = [n for n in nodes if n.id in needed]) and model_copy(deep=False) does not copy them, so "pruned config IS full_graph config object: True", and after collect_artifacts "full_graph config['artifact_path'] after bundling = 'model.cbm'". BUT every claimed HARM is refuted by the same run: (B) two collect_artifacts calls on the same object both yield key 'score__model.cbm' and config value 'model.cbm' — idempotent, not call-order dependent (the claim itself concedes "the key is stable here"); the repro_strategy's required assertion ("differing intermediate state / depends on call order") is false. (C-manifest) the mutation is intentional (line 100 comment: "Patch config so the scorer can build a matching artifact key"); the manifest serializes the mutated pruned_graph, the runtime reloads fresh, and _remap_artifact (src/haute/deploy/_scorer.py:270-287, key = f"{node_id}__{Path(raw_path).name}") resolved the bundled model correctly: "_remap_artifact resolved = ...downloaded_model.cbm". (C-key) _remap_artifact keys on Path(raw_path).name which is basename-invariant, so deep path and basename collapse to the SAME key 'score__model.cbm'. Grep over src/haute/deploy confirms NO consumer resolves config['artifact_path'] as a real filesystem path after the mutation (the actual download at _bundler.py:95 uses the pre-mutation local variable artifact_path). resolve_config re-parses from disk via parse_pipeline_file (line 543) every call, so it is re-runnable. No wrong value or behavior is demonstrable.
verdict.repro_outcome: Exit 0. Sub-claim A (in-memory shared mutation leaks to full_graph): CONFIRMED true. Sub-claim B (non-idempotent / call-order dependent): REFUTED — keys and config value identical across two calls. Sub-claim C (downstream consumer sees wrong value): REFUTED — _remap_artifact resolves correctly from the basename manifest config, and deep-path vs basename produce identical artifact keys. The claim's predicted failure does not materialize.
verdict.blast_radius: None observable today. The mutation is contained: the only value consumed downstream is config['artifact_path'] under Path(...).name (basename-invariant) or via fresh manifest reload. No code path resolves the post-mutation value as a real path, and resolve_config re-parses from disk so re-runs are unaffected. It is a latent maintainability smell (silent shared-state write across the full/pruned graph boundary) that would only become a real bug if a future consumer started treating config['artifact_path'] as a resolvable relative path on the in-memory full_graph.
verdict.recommended_fix: Optional hardening only (no current bug): instead of mutating the shared dict at _bundler.py:101, write to a fresh dict on a copied node, e.g. compute basename = Path(artifact_path).name locally for the artifact_name, and if the manifest must carry the basename, do it via node.data.model_copy(update={"config": {**config, "artifact_path": basename}}) and rebuild pruned_graph.nodes (mirroring _scorer._resolve_runtime_graph_paths), so full_graph is never touched. Add a regression test asserting full_graph.nodes[i].data.config['artifact_path'] is unchanged after collect_artifacts.
verdict.coordinate_risk: Low. _bundler.py / _config.py sit in the deploy subsystem; the current branch is wave-2-cache-integrity (cache work), so light overlap risk, but since this is a refuted/low-priority nit no coordination is warranted.

claim.title: Executor resolves pipeline config file paths with enforce_project_root defaulting False (prefer='project'), unlike HTTP routes which pass True — arbitrary-file read at execution if a graph's config is attacker-influenced
claim.location: src/haute/execution.py:178-184 and 405-413 (resolve_runtime_file_path(..., prefer='project') with enforce_project_root default False); src/haute/_path_resolution.py:70-133; contrast src/haute/routes/json_cache.py:149-154,167-172 and src/haute/routes/pipeline.py:148-152 (enforce_project_root=True)
claim.failure_scenario: resolve_runtime_file_path returns an absolute path unchecked when enforce_project_root=False (line 89-93 returns resolved without the is_relative_to(root) gate). The executor's path-rewriting (canonical_dataframe_execution_graph and _runtime_path_from_graph_config) calls it with the default False, then read_data_source/scan_parquet opens the resolved path. The HTTP route layer deliberately passes enforce_project_root=True. Any code path that builds a PipelineGraph from non-trusted config and runs it through the executor (an imported/shared pipeline graph JSON, a future route that constructs a graph from request data and executes before a route-level path check, or the deploy scorer which resolves graph paths via _resolve_runtime_graph_paths with no containment) can read/scan arbitrary host files (e.g. '/etc/passwd', secrets). The asymmetry means the containment invariant relied on at the route boundary is absent at the execution boundary.
claim.repro_strategy: Call resolve_runtime_file_path('/etc/passwd', source_file='/proj/pipe.py', prefer='project') (defaults) and assert it returns Path('/etc/passwd') with no ValueError, versus the same call with enforce_project_root=True raising. Then build a minimal dataSource node with config path pointing outside project_root and execute the graph, asserting the out-of-root file is read.

verdict.repro_outcome: PASS (exit 0) - all four sinks confirmed. [A] resolve_runtime_file_path('/outside/secret.csv', source_file=<in-root>, prefer='project') returns the out-of-root path verbatim; the same call with enforce_project_root=True raises ValueError ('resolves outside the project root'). [B] canonical_dataframe_execution_graph (the executor's path-rewrite step) keeps the out-of-root absolute dataSource path unchanged. [C] read_data_source(config) ACTUALLY READS the out-of-root file (col_a=['SECRET_VALUE']); _validate_source_path admits it (it only blocks '..' components and scheme://, never enforces is_relative_to(root) for absolute paths). [D] _validate_runtime_input_paths rejects the identical out-of-root graph with HTTP 403, while modelling.py (train) and optimiser.py LACK that guard and pipeline.py has it.
verdict.evidence: Core asymmetry confirmed in code + execution. _path_resolution.py:89-93: when raw.is_absolute(), the path is returned after resolve() and the is_relative_to(root) gate runs ONLY if enforce_project_root is True; the param defaults False (line 77). execution.py:178-184 (canonical_dataframe_execution_graph) and 405-413 (_runtime_path_from_graph_config) call resolve_runtime_file_path(raw, source_file=graph.source_file, prefer='project') with NO enforce_project_root, so absolute out-of-root paths survive into config['path']. The read path read_data_source -> build_data_source_adapter -> _read_flat_file -> read_source (_io.py:493) gates only on _validate_source_path (_io.py:141-147), which rejects scheme:// and '..' but NOT absolute out-of-root paths; the only is_relative_to(root) check (validate_project_path, _sandbox.py:60-72) is wired into load_external_object (_io.py:570-572), NOT into the flat-file scan_csv/scan_parquet/read_json reader. Routes pipeline.py:148-152 (and json_cache.py:149-154/167-172) deliberately pass enforce_project_root=True, and pipeline.py/explore.py call _validate_runtime_input_paths before executing (pipeline.py:410,512,725; explore.py:24). REACHABILITY IS STRONGER THAN THE CLAIM STATED: the train route modelling.py:50-57 (/api/modelling/train -> TrainService.start, _train_service.py:416/868) and the optimiser route optimiser.py:1106-1114 (/api/optimiser/solve -> OptimiserSolveService -> execute_lazy_graph, _optimiser_service.py:4263) execute request-supplied body.graph through the path-resolving executor and DO NOT call _validate_runtime_input_paths (confirmed: zero matches for the guard in modelling.py and _optimiser_service.py; flatten_graph and TrainService._validate_config perform no path containment). So a crafted TrainRequest/OptimiserSolveRequest with a dataSource/apiInput/externalFile node whose config.path is an absolute out-of-root path (e.g. a sibling secret parquet/csv) is read during execution. Minor correction to the claim's pointers: deploy/_scorer.py:212 _resolve_runtime_graph_paths does NOT use resolve_runtime_file_path and only rewrites RELATIVE paths (absolute pass through), and the deploy graph is operator-trusted (baked into the container, request supplies only input_df), so the deploy channel is a weak example; the train/optimiser routes are the real reachable channel.
verdict.blast_radius: Any caller that executes a request-supplied PipelineGraph without the route-level _validate_runtime_input_paths guard: confirmed at /api/modelling/train and /api/optimiser/solve (and the optimiser setup path). A dataSource/apiInput/externalFile/optimiserApply-artifact node with an absolute path escaping the project root is resolved unchanged and opened by Polars scan_csv/scan_parquet/read_json. This yields (1) arbitrary-file read for any host file the format reader can parse (scan_csv reads arbitrary text as a single-column frame; the repro returned clean content), the bytes then flowing into training/solve/preview output, and (2) a file-probe / large-file-read DoS primitive for other files. Practical impact is gated by the deployment trust model: haute is a localhost single-user pricing GUI/server, so a same-user attacker gains little (they can already read their own files); the exposure becomes material only if the API is network-reachable, multi-tenant, or hit via browser request forgery (CSRF). The pipeline/preview/explore/sink/trace routes are NOT affected (they enforce containment).
verdict.recommended_fix: Make project-root containment a property of the EXECUTION boundary, not just the route boundary, so it cannot be bypassed by any current or future executor caller. Smallest robust change: flip the executor's two resolve_runtime_file_path calls (execution.py:178-184 and 405-413) to pass enforce_project_root=True (they already supply source_file so project_root is inferred), and add the same is_relative_to(root) gate to the flat-file read path in _io.read_source / _validate_source_path (reject absolute paths outside _get_project_root for source reads, matching load_external_object). Belt-and-braces: add _validate_runtime_input_paths (or a shared pre-execution validator) to the train and optimiser route handlers (modelling.py /train, optimiser.py /solve and setup) so request graphs are validated identically to /pipeline/*. Add a failing test first per CLAUDE.md: a TrainRequest/OptimiserSolveRequest with an out-of-root source path must 403/raise, mirroring tests/test_pipeline_runtime_path_validation.py. Do NOT add a silent fallback - fail loudly with the existing 'resolves outside the project root' ValueError/403.
verdict.coordinate_risk: Yes - hot area. The fix touches src/haute/execution.py and src/haute/_path_resolution.py (and _io.read_source), which sit on the current branch wave-2-cache-integrity's cache-key/execution-canonicalisation path; canonical_dataframe_execution_graph feeds dataframe cache keys, so changing path resolution there can shift fingerprints and must be coordinated with in-flight cache-integrity work. The train/optimiser route guard additions are lower-risk and isolated to routes/. Recommend landing the executor/_io containment change with the cache-integrity owner aware, since resolved-path changes ripple into cache keys.

claim.title: available_ram_bytes reads host /proc/meminfo MemAvailable (ignores cgroup memory limits) and silently falls back to a fixed 4 GiB, driving wrong downsample decisions in containers/CI
claim.location: src/haute/_ram_estimate.py:51-126 (available_ram_bytes); 832-998 (estimate_safe_training_rows uses available*safety_factor for the downsample threshold)
claim.failure_scenario: available_ram_bytes returns the host's MemAvailable on Linux, which under a cgroup/container memory limit reflects the NODE's free memory, not the container's cap. On a 256 GiB node with a 4 GiB container cgroup limit, the estimator sees ~250 GiB usable, decides the dataset fits, and training OOM-kills inside the container — exactly the OOM the module exists to prevent. Conversely, if every detection path fails (sandboxed CI with /proc blocked, no sysconf, non-Windows) it returns a fixed 4 GiB, which on a real 64 GiB box causes needless aggressive downsampling — the model trains on _MIN_SAFE_ROWS-floored sample and prices are derived from a silently truncated training set. Because the estimate is used to choose safe_row_limit, both directions corrupt the training input without a loud failure (only a warning log).
claim.repro_strategy: Monkeypatch open('/proc/meminfo') and os.sysconf to raise, on a non-win32 platform, and assert available_ram_bytes() == 4*1024**3 regardless of true RAM. Separately, with a parquet source of known rows/cols, assert estimate_safe_training_rows downsamples (was_downsampled True, safe_row_limit floored to _MIN_SAFE_ROWS) purely because available collapsed to 4 GiB — i.e. the decision flips on the fallback, not on real capacity.

verdict.evidence: Ran review/02-findings/repro/platform__ram-estimate-cgroup-blind-and-4gib-fallback.py against the real haute._ram_estimate code. [A] With sys.platform='freebsd13', open() and os.sysconf patched to raise, available_ram_bytes() returned EXACTLY 4294967296 (4.00 GiB) -- a fixed fallback, host-RAM-blind, only a logger.warning('available_ram_fallback_4gib') is emitted (no raise; src/haute/_ram_estimate.py:114-126). This matches the pre-existing test test_ultimate_fallback_returns_4gib. [B] Identical synthetic graph (2,000,000-row parquet source, n_columns=200 via selected_columns; peak=8.94 GiB): at available=64 GiB -> was_downsampled=False, safe_row_limit=None; at available=4 GiB (the fallback) -> was_downsampled=True, safe_row_limit=626,349, truncating the 2,000,000-row training set. The decision flips SOLELY on the available-RAM value (estimate_safe_training_rows lines 850, 952, 966-980 compute usable=available*safety_factor and downsample when peak>usable). Cgroup-blind half is code-trace: lines 67-70 read /proc/meminfo MemAvailable, which on Linux reflects the host node, NOT the container's cgroup cap; a Grep across all of src/ found ZERO references to cgroup / memory.max / memory.limit_in_bytes / /sys/fs/cgroup -- no guard exists, so a 256 GiB node with a 4 GiB cgroup limit over-estimates usable RAM and OOM-kills inside the container. The estimate is consumed directly: src/haute/routes/_train_service.py:719 `row_limit = ram_est.safe_row_limit` with no re-validation against true container memory.
verdict.repro_outcome: PASS (claim reproduced). Output: "[A] available_ram_bytes()...= 4294967296 bytes (4.00 GiB); expected 4294967296"; "[B] @64GiB: was_downsampled=False safe_row_limit=None total_rows=2000000"; "[B] @4GiB : was_downsampled=True safe_row_limit=626349 total_rows=2000000"; "REPRO RESULT: CLAIM REPRODUCED". Nuance vs claim wording: safe_row_limit at 4 GiB was 626,349 (the dataset only mildly exceeds usable@4GiB), NOT literally _MIN_SAFE_ROWS=500; the _MIN_SAFE_ROWS floor (line 980) binds only at extreme low RAM, already covered by the existing test_safe_row_limit_respects_minimum (available=1). The load-bearing claim -- the downsample decision flips False->True purely on the fallback/wrong RAM value, truncating real training input -- is demonstrated exactly.
verdict.blast_radius: available_ram_bytes() is the single source of truth for the only OOM-prevention safety net guarding all model training (estimate_safe_training_rows) and is also consumed by _execution_admission.py adaptive memory-policy sizing. Both error directions silently corrupt the training run with no loud failure: (1) cgroup-blind over-estimate on a large node with a small container cap -> in-container OOM-kill (the exact failure the module exists to prevent); (2) 4 GiB fallback under-estimate on a real large box (sandboxed CI with /proc blocked, no sysconf, non-Windows) -> needless aggressive downsampling, model trains on a silently truncated sample and prices derive from it. Only manifests in containerized/cgroup-limited or sandboxed-CI deployments, not the default dev/Windows path.
verdict.recommended_fix: In available_ram_bytes(), before reading /proc/meminfo MemAvailable, detect a cgroup memory limit and take the min of host-available and (cgroup-limit minus current usage): read cgroup v2 /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max + memory.current (treat 'max' as unlimited), falling back to cgroup v1 /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.limit_in_bytes + memory.usage_in_bytes. Clamp the returned value to min(MemAvailable, cgroup_headroom). Separately, reconsider the silent 4 GiB fallback: per the project's no-silent-fallback guidance, prefer raising (or surfacing an explicit, caller-visible 'RAM undetectable' signal) when every detection path fails on a non-Windows platform, rather than fabricating 4 GiB that silently drives downsampling. Add tests that monkeypatch the cgroup files to assert the container cap wins over a large host MemAvailable, and that the undetectable case fails loudly instead of returning a fixed value.
verdict.coordinate_risk: Moderate. _ram_estimate.py is a focused module, but _execution_admission.py (same memory subsystem, calls available_ram_bytes for adaptive/fixed/strict memory-policy sizing) is actively evolving and an in-flight memory-policy feature could be editing the RAM-detection contract concurrently. The work sits on branch wave-2-cache-integrity. Coordinate the fix with whoever owns the adaptive memory policy so the cgroup-aware value is consistent across both consumers.

claim.title: Local session token is accepted as a URL query parameter for websockets and absent-Origin is treated as trusted, weakening the local-auth boundary to a single leakable secret
claim.location: src/haute/_local_security.py:160-163 (_query_token), 194-203 (websocket_rejection_reason accepts token from query params), 142-147 (_is_local_origin returns True when Origin header absent)
claim.failure_scenario: websocket_rejection_reason accepts the session token from the haute_session_token query parameter (line 200-201). URLs with query strings routinely land in server access logs, browser history, Referer headers, and proxy logs, so the websocket auth secret leaks into low-trust sinks. Combined with _is_local_origin returning True whenever the Origin header is missing (any non-browser client / tool that omits Origin bypasses the Origin defence entirely), the token is the sole gate, and it is exposed in a query string. An attacker who reads a log (or a malicious local process that scrapes the URL) can replay it to drive the local server's pipeline-execution and file-write endpoints. The HTTP path does not accept the token via query (header only), so this is specifically the websocket surface plus the absent-Origin allowance.
claim.repro_strategy: Call websocket_rejection_reason(Headers({}), QueryParams({'haute_session_token': local_session_token()})) and assert it returns None (auth passes) despite no header and no Origin — proving the token-in-query path authorizes. Assert _is_local_origin(Headers({})) is True (absent Origin trusted).

verdict.evidence: Executed repro (all 6 checks PASS) confirms the bare MECHANICS the claim cites: [PASS] A: websocket_rejection_reason(Headers({}), QueryParams({haute_session_token: <valid>})) -> None (authorized, no header, no Origin); [PASS] B: _is_local_origin(Headers({})) -> True (absent Origin trusted). Negative controls also pass: wrong/absent token rejected (C/D), and a PRESENT foreign Origin is rejected even WITH a valid query token (E). So the token-in-query path and absent-Origin allowance exist exactly as described. HOWEVER the claimed SECURITY DEFECT (token leaks to low-trust sinks, weakening the boundary to "a single leakable secret") is refuted on the actual loopback/single-user threat model: (1) The token NEVER appears in a navigable/address-bar URL — it is injected into the page via window.__HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN__ in an inline <script> (src/haute/server.py:710) or VITE_HAUTE_SESSION_TOKEN (src/haute/cli/_serve.py:412), so the "browser history" sink does not apply; only the ws:// handshake URL carries it, and browsers do not record WebSocket handshakes in history. (2) "Referer headers" / "proxy logs" do not apply: a ws://localhost handshake URL is the connection target (never sent as Referer to a third party) and loopback traffic does not traverse a proxy. (3) "Server access logs" is the only partially-true sink, but it is the LOCAL server's own stdout — same trust boundary as the process that minted the token (secrets.token_urlsafe(32), 256-bit, _local_security.py:30). Dev mode SUPPRESSES access logging (uvicorn.run(..., log_level="warning"), _serve.py:471); prod mode (_serve.py:502-506) leaves uvicorn's default access log on but still only to local stdout. An attacker who can read that log already has same-user local access and can read HAUTE_LOCAL_SESSION_TOKEN from the process environment (set by ensure_local_session_token_env, line 60) — the query string adds no new capability. (4) Token-in-query is NECESSARY: the browser WebSocket API has no request-header support (frontend forced to use it, useWebSocketSync.ts:108-110). (5) Absent-Origin=trusted is the CORRECT CSRF design, not a bypass: Origin defends the browser confused-deputy vector (browsers always send Origin, so a malicious page is always caught at E), while the 256-bit token defends non-browser clients. The behavior is documented (docstring lines 1-7) and explicitly tested as INTENDED (tests/test_security_gaps.py:1094-1137, including test_ws_sync_* using ?haute_session_token=... and test_ws_testclient_host_without_origin_still_requires_session_token). Net: mechanics real, asserted impact does not hold under the loopback single-user model.
verdict.repro_outcome: Script ran to completion with all 6 assertions PASS (no SystemExit). Confirmed: (A) query-token authorizes WS with no header/no Origin -> None; (B) _is_local_origin(no Origin) -> True; (C) wrong query token -> "Missing or invalid Haute session token"; (D) no token anywhere -> rejected; (E) foreign Origin rejected even with valid query token -> "Origin is not trusted..."; (F) header token authorizes -> None. The mechanics reproduce; the claimed low-trust leakage impact is what fails to hold (judged by code-trace of leak sinks + uvicorn log config), so the finding is refuted rather than confirmed.

claim.title: safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load allow the entire numpy/sklearn/scipy/pandas/joblib trees, so __reduce__ payloads of allowlisted classes still drive object construction from externalFile pickle paths
claim.location: src/haute/_sandbox.py:346-413 (_ALLOWED_PICKLE_PREFIXES whole-package single-segment entries; _pickle_global_is_allowed prefix match), 416-473 (safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load); reachable via src/haute/_io.py load_external_object
claim.failure_scenario: The RestrictedUnpickler only filters find_class by module prefix and allows every name under numpy/sklearn/scipy/pandas/joblib/collections. Pickle reduce machinery still executes for those classes, and many allowlisted callables are construction-capable (e.g. numpy multiarray reconstructors, sklearn estimator __setstate__, pandas/joblib reducers), so a crafted .pkl using only allowlisted globals can drive non-trivial object construction / state injection during load. load_external_object exposes this to any externalFile node whose path passes validate_project_path — i.e. a malicious .pkl placed in-project (or via a path that resolves inside the root) is only weakly contained. The module docstring concedes payloads must be 'trusted', but the deploy/exec paths treat in-project artifacts as automatically loadable. This is loud-or-exploit (not silent mispricing), but the allowlist is broad enough that the restriction provides little real isolation.
claim.repro_strategy: Code-trace: enumerate that single-segment prefixes ('numpy','sklearn','scipy','pandas','joblib') permit arbitrary qualnames; show a pickle opcode stream using only numpy.core.multiarray._reconstruct (allowlisted) constructs an attacker-chosen array/object, and that find_class returns it without further checks. Demonstrate the call reaches via load_external_object for an externalFile node path inside project root.

verdict.evidence: Ran review/02-findings/repro/platform__sandbox-restricted-unpickler-broad-allowlist.py — all 14 checks PASSED. Part 1: _pickle_global_is_allowed returns True for arbitrary deep qualnames under the single-segment entries (numpy/sklearn/scipy/pandas/joblib), e.g. ('numpy.core.multiarray','_reconstruct'), ('sklearn.some.deeply.nested.module','AnyName'), ('numpy','literally_anything_at_all') -> True; only 'numpy_evil' is rejected (the lone narrowing). Part 2: a pickle whose globals are ONLY ('numpy._core.multiarray','_reconstruct') and ('numpy','ndarray') round-tripped attacker-chosen bytes through safe_unpickle — 'construct::attacker-bytes-materialised: reconstructed bytes == b"\xde\xad\xbe\xef\xca\xfe\xba\xbe"', all emitted globals allowlisted=True. Part 3: a forged LinearRegression with injected coef_=[1234.5,-9999.0], intercept_=42.0 loaded via safe_joblib_load and drove output 'predict([[1,0]]) -> 1276.5 (== forged 1234.5+42)'. So construction/state-injection from allowlisted trees is real and the restriction does nothing against it. Code-trace confirms the os.system/subprocess/posix RCE class IS still blocked (tests/test_sandbox.py:140-225 pass; find_class at _sandbox.py:405-413 rejects non-allowlisted modules), so the claim's 'little real isolation' is an overstatement — the catastrophic RCE class is contained; only allowlisted ML-library object construction is not. The module + both function docstrings (_sandbox.py:1-23, 398-403, 419-421, 438-441) EXPLICITLY document pickle payloads as trusted inputs with no untrusted-safety guarantee, so the construction-capability is acknowledged design. Reachability is real but operator-authored: load_external_object (_io.py:563-575) -> safe_unpickle/safe_joblib_load reached from _builders.py:723 (node 'path' from authored graph) and deploy/_scorer.py:510 (remapped MLflow bundle artifact via _remap_artifact), gated only by validate_project_path; the same externalFile node also feeds arbitrary 'code' to _exec_user_code, a strictly larger capability than pickle state-injection. content_hash (_io.py:574) is a cache key only — no signature/integrity check — but no untrusted-to-trusted crossing is demonstrated. Verdict: factual mechanism real/reproduced; security impact is a documented defense-in-depth limitation at its stated trust boundary, hence severity low.
verdict.repro_outcome: All 14 assertions PASSED. The allowlist permits arbitrary qualnames under whole-package entries; safe_unpickle reconstructed an attacker-chosen numpy array (bytes 0xdeadbeefcafebabe) and safe_joblib_load reconstructed a fully attacker-forged LinearRegression (coef_=[1234.5,-9999.0], intercept_=42.0) whose state drove predict()=1276.5 — all using ONLY allowlisted globals, while RCE-class globals (os.system/subprocess/posix) remain blocked. Mechanism reproduced; the failure asserted on specific attacker-chosen VALUES, not merely that something raised.
verdict.blast_radius: All pickle/joblib artifact loads via load_external_object: externalFile nodes (build-time graph execution in _builders.py and codegen) and deploy-time scoring (deploy/_scorer.py remapped MLflow bundle artifacts). A construction-capable/state-forged artifact already trusted into the project/bundle loads without object-level restriction. No silent mispricing across unrelated nodes; impact is confined to whatever the loaded artifact's state feeds (e.g. a forged estimator's predictions). RCE beyond the documented trusted-input boundary is NOT demonstrated — os/subprocess/eval globals stay blocked.
verdict.recommended_fix: Treat as defense-in-depth hardening, not an emergency. Option A (tighten allowlist): replace the broad single-segment package prefixes with an explicit set of expected (module, qualname) pairs for the concrete model/data classes actually loaded (e.g. specific sklearn estimators, numpy._core.multiarray._reconstruct/ndarray/dtype, scipy.sparse matrix types), so unexpected qualnames under those trees are rejected. Option B (authenticity): add integrity/provenance verification for loadable artifacts (sign the bundle manifest or pin an allowlist of artifact content hashes at build/registration time; content_hash is currently cache-only) so only operator-blessed pickles load. Option C (format): migrate model persistence to a non-code-bearing format (e.g. ONNX / explicit JSON+array files) for the estimator state where feasible. Update the docstrings to state the residual construction/state-injection capability explicitly if the trusted-input posture is kept.
verdict.coordinate_risk: Low-to-moderate. _sandbox.py restricted unpickler and _io.load_external_object sit in a security-sensitive but stable area; current branch is wave-2-cache-integrity and recent commits touch rating-optimiser/projection regressions, not the sandbox/unpickler. Tightening the allowlist (_ALLOWED_PICKLE_PREFIXES) could surface real model classes currently relying on whole-tree allowance, so any change must be co-developed with the deploy/_scorer and modelling artifact-loading tests to avoid breaking legitimate sklearn/catboost/xgboost/lightgbm loads.

claim.title: _validation_cache is an unbounded module-global keyed by the full code string; long-lived servers accumulate one entry per distinct previewed/traced code fragment
claim.location: src/haute/_sandbox.py:273-323 (_validation_cache dict, _validate_user_code_cached stores (code, allow_imports) -> True forever, no eviction/maxsize)
claim.failure_scenario: Every distinct safe code string (and allow_imports flag) that passes AST validation is inserted into _validation_cache and never evicted. In a long-running server where each node edit/preview/trace produces a new code fragment (which it does — each keystroke-saved variation is a new key), the dict grows without bound, retaining the full source text of every fragment ever validated. This is a slow memory leak proportional to editing activity. It is guarded by a lock so it is not corrupted, but it is unbounded. No correctness impact on prices; a resource/robustness issue for long-lived processes.
claim.repro_strategy: Call validate_user_code on N distinct safe code strings (e.g. f'df = df.with_columns(pl.lit({i}))' for i in range(10000)) and assert len(haute._sandbox._validation_cache) == 10000 (monotonic growth, no cap/eviction).

verdict.evidence: Executed repro fed 10,000 distinct safe fragments (`df = df.with_columns(pl.lit({i}))`) through `haute._sandbox.validate_user_code`. Output: baseline cache size 0 -> after 10000, net growth EXACTLY 10000, cache type `dict`, no `max_size`/`maxsize`/`cache_info`. Under the identical N-distinct-key load, the codebase's own `LRUCache(max_size=128)` capped at 128. Code trace confirms: `_validation_cache: dict[tuple[str, bool], bool] = {}` (_sandbox.py:273) and the only writer is `_validation_cache[cache_key] = True` (line 323) under a lock — no eviction, no maxsize, no popitem, no `.clear()` in production. Whole-repo grep shows the only production reads/writes are the three lines in _sandbox.py (273, 313, 323); the only other touchers are tests, which pop individual keys for state reset and assert correctness (hits/misses), never a bound. No periodic sweep or shutdown clear exists. By contrast the sibling `_feature_validation_cache` is an `LRUCache` with `_clear_feature_validation_cache()`/`evict_where` and a dedicated bounded-behavior test file — confirming a bound is the established pattern this cache violates.
verdict.repro_outcome: PASS (exit 0). All assertions held: net growth == 10000 (monotonic, no eviction); cache is a bare `dict` with no `max_size`; codebase's bounded `LRUCache(max_size=128)` capped at 128 under the same load. Demonstrates the specific wrong behavior (unbounded retention of full source text of every distinct validated fragment) vs. the expected bounded behavior, not merely "something raised".
verdict.blast_radius: Long-lived server processes only. The server preview/trace path (src/haute/routes/_train_service.py and the executor) calls validate_user_code on each node edit/preview/trace; each distinct keystroke-saved code variation is a new `(code, allow_imports)` key retained forever, so the dict grows with cumulative editing activity, holding the full source text of every fragment ever validated. Memory grows slowly and unboundedly proportional to distinct fragments. The CLI train path (src/haute/cli/_train.py) is short-lived and unaffected. No correctness impact on prices; purely a resource/robustness issue. Magnitude is modest per entry (source strings are small), so it is a slow leak, not a crash risk in normal use.
verdict.recommended_fix: Replace the bare module-global `dict` with the codebase's existing bounded `haute._lru_cache.LRUCache` (mirroring `_feature_validation_cache`), e.g. `_validation_cache: LRUCache[tuple[str, bool], bool] = LRUCache(max_size=...)`, using `.get(key) is not None`/`.put(key, True)` in `_validate_user_code_cached`. Choose a cap consistent with the preamble cache default (128) or larger if validation churn warrants. LRUCache is already thread-safe, so the explicit `_validation_cache_lock` around get/put can be dropped (or kept; harmless). claim.title: fetch_and_cache atomic Path.replace can raise PermissionError on Windows when a concurrent reader has the cache parquet open (no FILE_SHARE_DELETE), turning a fetch into a 500 instead of a clean overwrite
claim.location: src/haute/_databricks_io.py:405-413 (tmp_path.replace(out_path) inside try/except BaseException which unlinks tmp and re-raises); read side src/haute/_databricks_io.py:437-448 (read_cached_table -> pl.scan_parquet holding the file)
claim.failure_scenario: fetch_and_cache writes a unique temp file then `tmp_path.replace(out_path)` to atomically publish. On Windows, os.replace/MoveFileEx onto a destination that another handle has open without FILE_SHARE_DELETE fails with PermissionError (ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED). read_cached_table returns pl.scan_parquet(p) which keeps the file open while a lazy plan is alive. If a pipeline run is reading the cached table (or another fetch's reader) while a fetch finishes, the replace raises, the except BaseException branch unlinks the temp and re-raises — the fetch fails with a non-domain error even though the data was complete. The code comments document a different Windows resolve() race but not this replace-vs-open race. Under the single-user model concurrency is rare, but the documented 'last finished fetch wins' guarantee does not hold on Windows under an active reader.
claim.repro_strategy: On Windows: create a cache parquet, open it via pl.scan_parquet(...).collect() held in a lazy frame / keep an OS handle open without share-delete, then call fetch_and_cache (mock the databricks cursor to stream one batch) for the same table and assert tmp_path.replace(out_path) raises PermissionError and the cache is not updated. On POSIX the same sequence succeeds, demonstrating the platform-specific gap.

verdict.repro_outcome: Ran on win32 / Polars 1.39.2 via `uv run`. Probe 3 (ground truth): an open OS handle without FILE_SHARE_DELETE (builtin open(dest,'rb')) makes os.replace(src,dest) raise PermissionError(13,'Access is denied'). Probe 4 (real code path): driving the actual fetch_and_cache with a mocked databricks cursor (one data batch + empty terminator => a COMPLETE fetch) while an OS handle is held -> fetch_returned=False, raised_type=PermissionError, is_permission_error=True, is_domain_error=False, cache_unchanged=True. So a complete fetch is turned into a raw non-domain 500-class error and the cache is NOT updated, exactly as the failure_scenario describes. HOWEVER the claim's STATED trigger is refuted: Probe 1 (held pl.scan_parquet lazy plan) = False (no handle), Probe 2 (held collected DataFrame) = False, and a forced gated in-flight collect (UDF holds the read open while replace is attempted) => replace SUCCEEDED, collect ok height=500000. Polars opens the parquet WITH FILE_SHARE_DELETE, so haute's own read_cached_table reader can never trigger the PermissionError.
verdict.evidence: Real bug confirmed at src/haute/_databricks_io.py:405 `tmp_path.replace(out_path)` inside `try/except BaseException` (lines 406-410: writer.close(); tmp_path.unlink(missing_ok=True); raise). Executed output: "probe3_oshandle_blocks_replace = True / probe3_err = PermissionError(13, 'Access is denied')"; end-to-end "fetch_returned=False ... is_permission_error=True ... cache_unchanged=True ... is_domain_error=False". REFUTATION of the claim's mechanism: the named reader read_cached_table -> pl.scan_parquet (lines 437-448) holds NO OS handle — "probe1_lazy_plan_blocks_replace = False", "probe2_collected_blocks_replace = False", and the gated forced-overlap test printed {'collect': 'ok height=500000', 'replace': 'SUCCEEDED'}, proving Polars uses FILE_SHARE_DELETE. haute's own read paths (scan_parquet; read_parquet_metadata via pyarrow at _polars_utils.py:301-314; grep for open()/mmap in _databricks_io.py = no matches) never open the cache without share-delete, so the codebase cannot self-collide. The code comment at lines 155-160 documents a different (resolve()) Windows race, not this one.

Scope: a single fetch_and_cache call (GUI "Fetch Data" route) surfaces a raw PermissionError 500 to the user and leaves the prior cache file unchanged; the complete fetched data is discarded. No corruption — the old cache stays intact and a retry once the foreign handle is released succeeds. Single-user desktop model makes a concurrent foreign handle uncommon, but AV/indexer/preview handles are plausible in practice.
verdict.recommended_fix: Make the publish step tolerant of the transient Windows lock: wrap `tmp_path.replace(out_path)` in a short bounded retry-with-backoff that catches PermissionError (ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED / errno EACCES) on win32 only, retrying the os.replace a few times over a fraction of a second; if it still fails, raise a domain FetchIntegrityError (HauteError subclass) with an actionable message ("a program is holding the cache file open; close it and re-fetch") instead of re-raising the raw OSError, and keep the existing tmp unlink only after exhausting retries. Do NOT change the success path. Optionally correct the docstring/comment to note the replace-vs-foreign-handle Windows caveat alongside the existing resolve() note. Note for the finding author: the claim's cited cause (pl.scan_parquet lazy reader keeping the file open) is incorrect — Polars uses FILE_SHARE_DELETE — so the fix must target foreign handles, not haute's own reader.

claim.title: Node-level _columns / _availableColumns are source-blind and are NOT invalidated when the active source changes; editors and edge-join validation then operate on the previously-previewed source's schema

Assert that the node's data._columns is unchanged (still source-A columns) and that getColumns()/edgeJoinValidation see source-A columns even though activeSource is now 'B'. No re-preview is triggered by the source change.

NO INVALIDATION: Toolbar.tsx:151 source-menu click calls only setActiveSource(s); useSettingsStore.ts:168 setActiveSource is `set({ activeSource: source })` — pure state write. The existing test usePipelineAPI.propagation.test.ts:294-336 confirms flipping activeSource mid-cascade has zero effect on stored columns — it neither cancels, redirects, nor clears. READ (stale consumption): NodePanel.tsx:879-880 reads node.data._availableColumns/_columns and passes them into ColumnsTab/GroupedColumnsTab (1025-1026, 1032-1033); ColumnsTab.tsx:24,48-66 builds the picker universe from these and writes selected_columns on toggle. NodePanel.tsx:646-653 + 468-476 derive upstreamColumns via collectColumnsFromEdges reading upstream _columns (source-blind), fed to RatingStepEditor (792) whose column universe is upstreamColumns.map(c=>c.name) (RatingStepEditor.tsx:282). edgeJoinValidation.ts:253-255 getColumns returns node.data._columns ?? []; used at 134-135 for baseColumns/joinColumns and validated via addColumnDiagnostics (153-155); invoked at SAVE time by findFirstInvalidEdgeJoin (usePipelineAPI.ts:752). claim.title: Preview LRU cache slot is keyed by nodeId alone while freshness depends on (structuralVersion, source, rowLimit); a node can hold at most one cached preview, so toggling source/rowLimit evicts the other context's preview and forces a full refetch each toggle
claim.location: frontend/src/stores/useNodeResultsStore.ts:95-100 (CachedPreview), 647-662 (setPreview overwrites slot [nodeId]), 664-672 (getPreview by nodeId); frontend/src/hooks/usePipelineAPI.ts:296-316,597-602 (matchesRequestContext / cross-context gating)
claim.failure_scenario: Single LRU slot per nodeId. Preview node X under source 'live' stores {data, source:'live'}. Switch to 'staging', preview X → setPreview overwrites slot X with {source:'staging'} (the 'live' preview is gone, even though MAX_CACHED_PREVIEWS=24 had room for both). Switch back to 'live': getPreview(X) returns the 'staging' entry; the source guard at usePipelineAPI.ts:306/598 sees cached.source('staging') !== snapshotSource('live') so it shows the loading state and refetches. Net effect: a node can never retain two sources'/rowLimits' previews simultaneously; every source/rowLimit toggle round-trip pays a full backend re-execution and a loading flash, and the documented invariant 'a node holds at most one cached preview across sources/rowLimits' is itself the defect. (Note: the cross-context guard does prevent painting the wrong-source rows, so this is a cache-thrash/UX correctness issue, not a wrong-rows paint.)
claim.repro_strategy: Store unit test: setPreview('n1', dataLive, 0, 'live', 1000); setPreview('n1', dataStaging, 0, 'staging', 1000); assert getPreview('n1').source==='staging' and that no 'live' entry survives (only one slot). Confirms single-context retention per node.

verdict.evidence:
The preview cache slot is keyed by nodeId alone, while freshness depends on (structuralVersion, source, rowLimit) — confirmed by exact source.

(1) Slot identity = nodeId only. useNodeResultsStore.ts:545 `previews: Record<string, CachedPreview>`; setPreview at 652-654 writes `{...s.previews, [nodeId]: { data, structuralVersion, source, rowLimit }}` — the key is `[nodeId]`; source/rowLimit are stored as VALUES inside the entry, never in the key. Contrast columnCache, which IS composite-keyed: line 632/639 `const key = source ? \`${sourceNodeId}:${source}\` : sourceNodeId`. The developers key-by-source for columns but not for previews — dispositive asymmetry.

(2) Overwrite collapses prior context. Existing passing test previewCache.test.ts:90-97 ("returns the latest preview when set multiple times") shows two setPreview('n1',…) leave exactly ONE entry (the last). So setPreview('n1',live,'live') then setPreview('n1',staging,'staging') destroys the 'live' entry. MAX_CACHED_PREVIEWS=24 is irrelevant: trimCacheByRecency only evicts when keys.length - maxEntries > 0 (523-525); there is only ever one key per node, so the cap never makes room for a second same-node entry.

(3) Lookup by nodeId only. getPreview signature has no source/rowLimit arg (571); body returns get().previews[nodeId] (665).

(4) Round-trip forces loading flash + refetch. In fetchPreviewImmediate: cached=getPreview(node.id) (305) returns surviving 'staging' entry; gate at 306 `cached.source === snapshotSource && cached.rowLimit === snapshotRowLimit` is FALSE ('staging'!=='live'), so else-branch 314-315 paints `status:"loading"` (the flash) and proceeds to previewNode({...}) (496) — full backend re-execution. matchesRequestContext (296-299) likewise never lets the API call be skipped on a context mismatch. The second call-site fetchPreview:598 has the identical guard and the same loading paint at 601.

Net: a node retains at most one preview across (source,rowLimit); every source/rowLimit toggle round-trip evicts the other context, shows a loading flash, and re-executes the backend despite 24-slot headroom. The claim's own caveat is correct — the 306/598 source guards prevent painting wrong-source rows, so this is cache-thrash/UX correctness, not a wrong-rows paint.
verdict.repro_outcome: Not executed: this is a frontend TS/React claim, so per method I produced a definitive code-trace instead of a Python repro. The claim's suggested store unit test (setPreview('n1', dataLive, 0, 'live', 1000) then setPreview('n1', dataStaging, 0, 'staging', 1000); assert getPreview('n1').source==='staging' and only one slot survives) is already effectively proven by the existing passing test previewCache.test.ts:90-97 plus the single-key trim logic at useNodeResultsStore.ts:523-525,652-654.
verdict.blast_radius: Every Preview/Data node previewed under more than one active source or row-limit. Each source/rowLimit toggle round-trip on a given node pays a redundant backend previewNode execution plus a "Executing pipeline…" loading flash, instead of an instant cache hit. No incorrect data is ever displayed (the 306/598 source+rowLimit guards block wrong-context painting), so this is a performance/UX regression, not data corruption. Impact scales with how often users flip activeSource/rowLimit while inspecting the same nodes.
verdict.recommended_fix: Compose the preview cache key the same way columnCache already does. Key previews by `${nodeId}|${source}|${rowLimit}` (or a small composite), have setPreview/getPreview accept (and getPreview match on) source+rowLimit, and bound the cache per-node-context via trimCacheByRecency. Update both call-site guards (usePipelineAPI.ts:306 and :598) to look up the context-specific entry rather than re-checking source/rowLimit on a single ambiguous slot. Keep clearNode/pinned-eviction working over the new key. Mirror the existing source-keyed column-cache tests (useNodeResultsStore.test.ts:1897+) with preview equivalents asserting two contexts for one node coexist and survive toggling.
verdict.coordinate_risk: High. The two touched files (frontend/src/stores/useNodeResultsStore.ts and frontend/src/hooks/usePipelineAPI.ts) are the core of the preview/column cache, and the current branch is `wave-2-cache-integrity` — exactly the cache-integrity area an in-flight wave is editing. claim.title: updateFrontierAfterSelect writes selectResult.total_objective / constraints / baselines / lambdas directly into the displayed SolveResult without the numericFrontierValue finite-number guard, while parseFrontierSelectResponse permits these to be undefined (and the TS type declares them required) — a backend that omits total_objective yields an undefined optimiser objective shown as the selected result
claim.location: frontend/src/stores/useNodeResultsStore.ts:877-893 (direct assignment of selectResult.total_objective, .constraints, .baseline_objective, .baseline_constraints, .lambdas with no numeric validation); frontend/src/types/guards.ts:1526-1530 (optionalNumber/optionalNumberRecord — permit undefined); frontend/src/api/types.ts:677-682 (FrontierSelectResponse declares total_objective: number, constraints: Record<string,number> as REQUIRED)
claim.failure_scenario: User clicks a frontier point. client.selectFrontierPoint POSTs and runs parseFrontierSelectResponse, which validates total_objective via optionalNumber — so a response object without total_objective (contract drift, or a partial/error-shaped 200) parses successfully with total_objective === undefined. updateFrontierAfterSelect takes the non-stale branch and builds result.total_objective = selectResult.total_objective = undefined (and constraints = selectResult.constraints possibly {}). Unlike the deriveSolveResultForFrontierPoint path — which runs numericFrontierValue on every field and throws on non-finite — this path performs NO numeric check, so OptimiserPreview renders an undefined/blank objective (or NaN in downstream arithmetic) as the authoritative result for the selected operating point. The fail-loud contract (CLAUDE.md) is bypassed precisely on the user-facing optimisation number.
claim.repro_strategy: Store unit test: completeSolveJob with a frontier (>=1 point with selectable summary), then call updateFrontierAfterSelect('n', 0, parseFrontierSelectResponse({status:'ok', point_index:0, constraints:{}, baseline_objective:0, baseline_constraints:{}, lambdas:{}, converged:true})) — i.e. total_objective omitted. Assert the parser does not throw and that solveResults['n'].result.total_objective is undefined (no finite-number guard fired).

verdict.evidence:
The claim's central premise — that parseFrontierSelectResponse "permits these to be undefined" and writes total_objective === undefined — is factually wrong. The guard the claim says is missing is effectively present via the parser's defaulting.

GUARD/REASON: optionalNumber and optionalNumberRecord do NOT permit undefined; they substitute defaults.

frontend/src/types/guards.ts:175-183 optionalNumber(parser, obj, key, defaultValue = 0): number { const value = obj[key]; return value === undefined ? defaultValue : expectNumber(...) }. Return type is `number`. For an omitted total_objective, value===undefined is true → returns 0 (defaultValue). expectNumber is never reached.

frontend/src/types/guards.ts:328-336 optionalNumberRecord(...): Record<string,number> with defaultValue={} → missing constraints/baseline_constraints/lambdas become {} (not undefined).

frontend/src/types/guards.ts:1526-1530 — parseFrontierSelectResponse uses exactly these for total_objective/constraints/baseline_objective/baseline_constraints/lambdas. The function (lines 1519-1561) has no early return; it always returns a fully populated object. So parsing {status:'ok', point_index:0, constraints:{}, baseline_objective:0, baseline_constraints:{}, lambdas:{}, converged:true} (total_objective omitted) yields total_objective === 0, NOT undefined.

useNodeResultsStore.ts:879-883 then writes result.total_objective = selectResult.total_objective = 0 (and constraints = {}). No undefined/NaN.

Render: OptimiserPreview.tsx:386,560,765 call formatNumber(result.total_objective); formatValue.ts:39-44 formatNumber(0) → Number.isInteger(0) → "0". UI shows "Objective: 0", a concrete number — not undefined/blank/NaN as failure_scenario claims.

The claim's stated repro assertion ("solveResults['n'].result.total_objective is undefined") would FAIL: actual value is 0. The predicted observable does not occur, and there is no fail-loud bypass producing an undefined optimiser objective.

Type consistency: since optionalNumber returns concrete number, the object satisfies FrontierSelectResponse.total_objective: number (required) with value 0; no undefined leaks, so the claimed type/runtime mismatch is also absent.

Separate, NOT-claimed nuance (does not rescue the claim): expectNumber (guards.ts:138-142) uses Number.isNaN not Number.isFinite, so an explicitly-present Infinity would pass the parser whereas numericFrontierValue (useNodeResultsStore.ts:255-259) uses Number.isFinite. But that is about an explicit Infinity value, not the omitted/undefined field the claim is built on (which short-circuits to 0 before expectNumber runs).
verdict.repro_outcome: Not executed (frontend/TS claim → code-trace per instructions). Vitest harness exists (frontend/vitest.config.ts, include limited to src/**/__tests__ and e2e/__tests__), but execution was unnecessary because the data flow is deterministic and fully traceable. If the claim's own repro were run, the asserted outcome (total_objective === undefined) would fail because optionalNumber returns 0 for a missing field.

claim.title: frontierConstraintValue resolves a constraint by falling back to the bare row[name] key on the open FrontierPoint record; a constraint whose name collides with a frontier-row metadata key (e.g. iterations, clamp_rate, converged, index) reads that unrelated field as the constraint value
claim.location: frontend/src/stores/useNodeResultsStore.ts:393-402 (frontierConstraintValue: total_<name> -> constraints.<name> -> bare <name>); 420-425 (deriveSolveResultForFrontierPoint applies it per constraint_names); frontend/src/api/types.ts:555-560 (FrontierPoint = Record<string, unknown> & {...} — open record carrying index/iterations/clamp_rate/converged/total_objective alongside per-constraint totals)

A ratebook/optimiser constraint legitimately named 'iterations' (or any name equal to one of those metadata keys) is not present as total_iterations or under constraints.iterations, so frontierConstraintValue falls through to row['iterations'] and returns the SOLVER ITERATION COUNT as that constraint's value. numericFrontierValue accepts it (it is a finite number), so no error is raised; the OptimiserPreview shows the iteration count as the constraint total for the selected frontier point. claim.repro_strategy: Unit test deriveSolveResultForFrontierPoint via completeSolveJob with frontier.constraint_names=['iterations'] and a point {total_objective:1, iterations:42} (no total_iterations, no constraints.iterations). verdict.evidence:
Two-layer adjudication. LAYER 1 (function mechanics) is true as written but LAYER 2 (real-world reachability of the "legitimate collision") is false, which refutes the finding's actual failure scenario.

Function mechanics (useNodeResultsStore.ts:393-402): frontierConstraintValue resolves total_<name> -> constraints.<name> -> bare row[name]. numericFrontierValue (256-258) accepts any finite number. So for the synthetic repro input {total_objective:1, iterations:42} with name='iterations' and no total_iterations/constraints.iterations, branch 3 returns [42,'iterations'] and deriveSolveResultForFrontierPoint yields result.constraints['iterations']===42. The repro's assert would pass — but only because the input is hand-crafted to omit total_iterations.

Reachability REFUTED by two independent guards that ensure total_<name> is ALWAYS present on the frontend payload, so branch 3 is dead for real data:
(1) Price-contour canonical frontier schema emits total_<name> for EVERY constraint. tests/test_optimiser_frontier_materialisation.py lines 31-33 and 173-188: "Order: threshold_<name> per constraint, total_objective, total_<name> per constraint, lambda_<name> per constraint, iterations, converged". .venv/.../price_contour/frontier.py:79-81 iterates df.columns matching col.startswith("total_") to recover constraint names, and reads selected_row["iterations"]/["converged"] as SEPARATE metadata columns. Thus a constraint named 'iterations' produces a distinct total_iterations column; the frontend hits branch 1 (total_iterations) and reads the correct constraint total. The iterations metadata (solver count) is never read as the constraint value.
(2) Backend normalisation backfills the collision before serialisation. src/haute/routes/_optimiser_limits.py:92-96 limited_frontier_payload: for each name in constraint_names, if total_<name> not in point and name in point, sets point[total_<name>]=point[name]. Every frontier payload reaching SolveResult.frontier goes through this function — the ONLY two producers are optimiser.py:1395 and _optimiser_service.py:2223 (grep confirmed). completeSolveJob (useNodeResultsStore.ts:705-714) passes rawFrontier.points straight through with NO frontend normalisation, but it does not need to: the payload already carries total_<name>.

Also: the frontend triple-key heuristic intentionally mirrors the backend's own _frontier_point_constraint_value (optimiser.py:468-477), which has the identical bare-name fallback — an accepted shared design, not an oversight. No reserved-constraint-name validation exists, but it is unnecessary because total_<name> is always materialised.
